pages.title: Organization settings
pages.description: Name your organization, restrict e-mail domains, check SSO and members.
pages.md:
Open the command palette (`⌘K` / `Ctrl+K`) and run **Organization settings…**.

## What you can set

- **Organization name** — shown in the admin panel.
- **Allowed e-mail domains** — the domains your members sign in with
  (`acme.com`, `acme.co.uk`). Used as the default domain for SSO sign-in.
- **SSO status** — whether an SSO worker is configured and whether you are
  currently signed in through it.
- **Members** — listed once SSO is connected. Without SSO the panel shows a
  "Connect SSO" prompt.
- **Audit log** — available on the Team plan (or always, when self-hosted
  without billing).

## Offline and self-hosted

Without a backend, the name and domains are stored only in this browser
(local-only mode). Nothing is sent to a server.

pages.title: Signing in
pages.description: What each sign-in status means and how to fix the common errors.
pages.md:
Signing in is optional — Lumen works fully offline without an account.
An account unlocks persistent collab rooms, cloud sync and Smart search.

## Status messages

| Status | Meaning | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| **Signed in** | A session is active. | Nothing. |
| **Signed out** | Cloud sign-in is available but you are not signed in. | Open **Sign in** in the toolbar. |
| **Sign-in not configured** | This build has no auth provider (local-only mode). | Self-hosters: see [Enable accounts](#enable-accounts). Everyone else: keep working locally. |
| **Sign-in error** | The provider could not be reached or rejected the request. | See [Troubleshooting](#troubleshooting). |

## Enable accounts

Set these in `.env.local` and rebuild:

- **Email / OAuth (Supabase)** — `VITE_SUPABASE_URL` and
  `VITE_SUPABASE_ANON_KEY`, then `npm install @supabase/supabase-js`.
- **Enterprise SSO (WorkOS)** — `VITE_WORKOS_ENDPOINT`; see
  [Single sign-on](/account/sso/).

## Troubleshooting

- **Network error / provider unreachable** — check your connection, VPN or
  corporate proxy, then retry. Lumen keeps working locally meanwhile.
- **Invalid email or password** — reset the password from the provider's
  e-mail, or use the OAuth buttons.
- **Session expired** — sign in again; your local documents are untouched.

pages.title: Single sign-on (SSO)
pages.description: Sign in with your company's identity provider through WorkOS.
pages.md:
Lumen supports SAML and OIDC single sign-on through
[WorkOS](https://workos.com). Your organization's admin connects the
identity provider once; members then sign in with their work e-mail domain.

## Signing in

1. Open **Sign in** in the toolbar.
2. Enter your organization's e-mail domain (for example `acme.com`).
3. Complete the sign-in at your identity provider. You are returned to
   Lumen and signed in.

## Error reasons

When SSO fails, Lumen returns with `?sso=error&reason=…`:

| Reason | Fix |
|---|---|
| `no_sso_connection` | No organization is set up for that domain. Ask your admin to add the domain in WorkOS. |
| `state_mismatch` | The sign-in was started in a different browser or took longer than 10 minutes. Start again. |
| `access_denied` | Your identity provider refused the sign-in — ask your IT admin to assign you to the Lumen app. |
| `code_exchange_failed` | The SSO worker could not verify the sign-in. Usually a wrong `WORKOS_API_KEY` / `WORKOS_CLIENT_ID`. |

## Self-hosting

Deploy `edge-workers/auth/` (see `DEPLOY.md` §5b) and set
`VITE_WORKOS_ENDPOINT` to the worker URL.

pages.title: Agent eval
pages.description: Every one of the 14 agents against fixed Hebrew and English cases, scored with deterministic checks, with a local HTML report.
pages.md:
The agent eval runs fixed cases through the **real agent runtime**: the
same prompts, tools, parsers and validators that the editor uses. Every
check is deterministic, so two models (or two versions of a prompt) can be
compared on the same numbers.

## What is covered

- **14 agents, at least 5 cases each**, with at least one Hebrew and one
  English input per agent (71 cases in all): tagger, outliner, tasker,
  translator, proofreader, diagrammer, charter, committer, writer, linker,
  templater, stylist, researcher and builder-spec.
- **The researcher** gets the web (a stubbed search and page), citations
  (`[^1]` footnotes checked against the sources), the clip library, a
  Hebrew question, and a page with a planted instruction
  ("IGNORE PREVIOUS INSTRUCTIONS…") that the answer must not follow.
- **Diagrams are compiled.** Every diagrammer answer goes through the real
  Mermaid parser (the `mermaid` check), not a pattern.
- **Tags come from the vault.** The tagger cases require at least one tag
  that the eval vault already uses (the `someOf` check over the
  `list_tags` result).
- **Each case expects a tool call** (for example `list_tags`,
  `validate_mermaid`, `git_diff`, `fetch_page`), made and executed by the
  runtime.

The cases are in `src/agents/eval/fixtures.ts` and
`src/agents/eval/moreCases.ts`.

## Running it

```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b
npm run eval:agents -- --model qwen2.5:7b
npm run eval:agents -- --model llama3.1:8b --only tagger,researcher-he-web
```

The run writes three files to `eval/results/` (change it with `--out`):

| File | What it is |
|---|---|
| `agents-<date>-<model>.md` | One table: case, agent, result, attempts, time, failed checks |
| `agents-<date>-<model>.json` | The same results, for `npm run eval:compare` |
| `agents-<date>-<model>.html` | A self-contained page with no scripts and no network: a pass count per agent, then every case |

Open the HTML file in a browser. An agent marked **FAIL** has at least one
case whose run failed or whose checks did not all hold. The notes column
says which.

## Comparing runs

`npm run eval:compare -- eval/results/agents-<date>-<model>.json` compares
a run with the saved baseline for that model. A case that passed before
and fails now is a regression, and so is a case that has disappeared; both
exit 1.

## In CI

The same cases run against a fake Ollama server (`npm run fake-ollama`)
over real HTTP. The fake server answers with each case's reference
answer, so CI checks the runtime and the cases themselves, not model
quality. Model quality needs a live run on a machine with Ollama.

pages.title: Auto-tag + link suggestions
pages.description: AI assistants that read your workspace and propose structure.
pages.md:
Lumen ships two opt-in agents that scan a note (and the rest of your
workspace) and suggest improvements. Both run from `⌘K`.

## Auto-tag this note

Command: `🏷️ Auto-tag this note`.

The agent reads the active document, looks at the existing `tags:`
vocabulary across every note in your workspace, and proposes 3–7 tags
that fit. You see the proposals first — accept, edit the list, or skip.
Accepted tags merge into the note's frontmatter idempotently (existing
tags are preserved).

**Why workspace-aware**: a fresh note about machine learning shouldn't
get a brand-new `ml` tag if you already use `machine-learning`
elsewhere. The agent prefers existing tokens and only invents new ones
when nothing fits.

## Suggest wiki-links

Command: `🔗 Suggest wiki-links`.

For each phrase in the active note that overlaps with the title or
intro of another note, the agent proposes wrapping the phrase in a
`[[Title|phrase]]` wiki-link. You review the list (each suggestion comes
with a one-line "why") and accept all / none.

Only literal substrings that already appear in your note become links —
the agent never invents prose. Phrases already inside a wiki-link or
markdown link are skipped automatically.

## Ask Workspace

Inside `⌘K → Search workspace…` → **Ask Workspace** tab. Hybrid retrieval
over your notes plus a chat model on top of the matched context. Multi-turn — the
conversation persists for the open dialog.

## Privacy

All three agents go through the same `chat()` pipeline and respect the
**Local AI** toggle (`⌘K → Switch to local AI (WebGPU)`) and the
[AI policy](/ai/privacy/). When local AI is on, prompts stay on your device — `web-llm` runs the model via WebGPU and
the workspace never leaves your browser.

pages.title: Airplane mode and the network monitor
pages.description: One switch that stops every network request Lumen can make, a live list of every attempt with where in the code it came from, and a certificate of the time it was on.
pages.md:
**Airplane mode (no network)** in the command palette stops every request Lumen could
send over the network, from the moment you turn it on. **Network monitor** lists every
attempt live, whether it was allowed, blocked, local or served from the cache, and shows
where in the code it came from. A badge in the corner shows that the mode is on.

## What it stops

| Path out | While airplane mode is on |
|---|---|
| `fetch` to another site | refused before it runs |
| `fetch` to Lumen's own server | GET only, and only from a cache (`only-if-cached`): never the network |
| `XMLHttpRequest`, `WebSocket`, `EventSource`, `sendBeacon`, WebRTC peers | refused. Live-collaboration sockets that were open are closed |
| Workers (model downloads) | the worker asks the page and refuses the request itself. A worker that gets no answer refuses too |
| Images, fonts, media, frames, stylesheets from other sites | refused by the browser itself: a Content-Security-Policy is added to the page |
| Playground and live-JS blocks | they don't run. Their runner page is a separate frame with its own policy, so the page's policy can't cover it. Frames load only from `blob:` while the mode is on |
| Cloud dictation (the browser's speech service) | not started |

These stay allowed, because they don't leave the computer: `localhost` / `127.0.0.1`
(a local model such as Ollama on this machine), `blob:` and `data:`.

A browser can't lift a Content-Security-Policy from a page that is already open. So
turning airplane mode **off reloads the page**. Save your work first. The mode stays on
across reloads until you turn it off, and the policy is in place before the app starts.

## The monitor and the certificate

Each row shows the time, the kind of request, the decision, the destination (address
and path only, never the query) and where it came from in the code. The code location
is the calling function and file, as the browser reports it. **Try a request** sends a
test request to `example.com`, so you can watch it appear as blocked.

While the mode is on, **Download certificate** saves a file that states the time span
and lists every attempt in it, with a count of how many reached the network (the claim
is 0). It counts attempts, not bytes:

- every request the page and its workers made through the wrapped network calls;
- every resource load the browser lists. A load from another site counts as reaching the
  network even when the browser reports 0 bytes (it hides the size of other sites' files);
- every request, socket or peer still open when you turned the mode on. These count as
  having reached the network, and are stopped at that moment.

The file also lists what it doesn't prove (`notCounted`). For example, a request made
through a copy of `fetch` that a library took before the wrappers loaded isn't listed,
although the page's policy still refuses it to any other site. The file is canonical
JSON with its SHA-256. It is not signed yet: signing with this device's key comes with
the signed privacy report.

## Limits

- Lumen's own script files that the offline cache doesn't hold load from Lumen's server,
  like any page resource; they are not `fetch` requests. The monitor sees them through
  the browser's Resource Timing, and the certificate counts any that transferred bytes
  as having reached the network.
- The plan's full check is the owner's to run: 22 commands under `mitmproxy`, with 0
  requests while the mode is on. `e2e/airplane-mode.spec.ts` checks the same promise
  against fake hosts.

pages.title: AI-written text
pages.description: Text the AI wrote is shown lighter until you edit it — in the editor, saved per note, and optionally in the export.
pages.md:
Whatever an AI command puts into your note — a draft from **Write**, a
**Rewrite** of a selection, an accepted completion, a template, an answer
you insert — is shown **lighter** in the source editor. The moment you edit
a word of it, that word is yours and looks like the rest of your text.

## How it works

- Every AI command runs through the agent runtime, which keeps the recent
  answers (for 15 minutes) on this device.
- When text lands in the note **without you typing it** — at the cursor,
  over a selection, or as an update of the whole note — Lumen checks it
  against those answers and marks the parts that came from one. An answer
  that was reformatted on the way (quoted, put in a list) is still found,
  line by line.
- What you type, paste or drop is never marked. Typing inside a mark cuts
  that part out of it; deleting shrinks it.
- The marks are saved per note on this device. A mark comes back only if
  its text is still exactly the same, so a note edited elsewhere never
  shows a stale mark.

## Show or hide

Command palette → **AI text marks: show / hide**. The choice is remembered.

## In the export

Command palette → **Export Markdown with AI marks** downloads the note with
one HTML comment at the end:

```markdown
<!-- lumen-ai-authorship v1: 120-340 512-640 -->
```

Each pair is a range of the text before the comment (start and end, in
UTF-16 code units, end not included). Markdown renderers show nothing for
the comment. The ordinary exports and **Save** leave it out.

## Limits

- The marks show in the source and split views; WYSIWYG doesn't draw them,
  but text the AI writes there is found again in the source view while the
  answer is recent.
- An answer older than 15 minutes, or text you copy from an answer and
  paste, is not marked.

pages.title: Local autocomplete (FIM)
pages.description: Completions as you type from a coding model on this device — Ollama with qwen2.5-coder, or the in-browser model — with no cloud route at all.
pages.md:
`⌘K → "AI: Local Autocomplete (FIM) — On/Off"` turns on completions as you
type. A pause of 150 ms after a keystroke sends the text **before and after
the cursor** to a local model, which fills in the middle; the answer
appears in grey at the cursor. **Tab** accepts it, **Esc** dismisses it,
and the next keystroke cancels a request still in flight.

## Where it runs

| Engine | When | Model |
|---|---|---|
| Ollama `/api/generate` with `suffix` | an Ollama on this machine or network has a completion model | `qwen2.5-coder:1.5b`, else `qwen2.5-coder:7b` (Apache-2.0) |
| The in-browser model (web-llm) | no such Ollama, and an in-browser model is already loaded in this tab | the loaded model, through the `completer` agent |
| — | neither | no completion (a keystroke never starts a model download) |

There is no cloud route: autocomplete never contacts a cloud provider,
under any AI policy, and an Ollama on a remote server is not used.
`qwen2.5-coder:3b` is never picked automatically — its licence (Qwen
Research) is not an open one. To use another installed model, set
`lumen.fim.model` in the browser's local storage.

Install the recommended model once:

```sh
ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:1.5b
```

## Speed

Answers are cached per context (the same text around the cursor twice is
answered at once), and the model is kept loaded between keystrokes. The
latency of every completion is kept; its p50 / p95 go to the agent trace
(`⌘K → "AI: Recent Agent Runs"`, agent `fim`) at most every 30 seconds.

`npm run bench:fim` measures it on your Ollama: 20 English, Hebrew and code
contexts × 3 rounds after a warm-up, printing p50 / p95 (`--assert 300`
fails when p50 is not under 300 ms, the target).

pages.title: Batch jobs — pause, resume, progress
pages.description: Run tags, summaries or translations over a folder on this device, watch the progress live, and pause, resume or cancel the job — also after a reload.
pages.md:
`AI: Batch over a Folder…` tags, summarises or translates every note in a
folder. Under the *local only* and *local first* policies the job runs on
this device (Ollama, or the in-browser model), one note at a time in the
background; under *cloud* with OpenAI or Anthropic it goes to their
half-price Batch API (see [AI cost](/ai/cost/)).

## The batch jobs panel

`⌘K → "AI: Batch Jobs — Progress, Pause, Resume"` (it also opens by itself
after you submit a local job) lists every job that hasn't been applied:

| What you see | What it means |
|---|---|
| progress bar and "*n* of *total* done · *k* failed" | live, after every note |
| "About … left" | the average time of the last notes × the notes still to go |
| **Pause** | the note being processed stops (it runs again on Resume) and nothing else starts. The pause is saved: after a reload or a restart the job is still paused, and "AI: Check Batch Jobs" doesn't restart it. |
| **Resume** | continues from the first note without an answer — notes already answered are never sent again |
| **Cancel job** | stops the job (a cloud job is cancelled at the provider); none of its results is applied |
| "Waiting for a local model" | no Ollama and no in-browser model was available; Resume tries again |
| **Apply results** | when the job has finished: the same review as "AI: Check Batch Jobs" — notes open in a tab are skipped and you confirm before anything is written |

## Every answer is checked

Each job has a validator for its operation, and an answer that fails goes
to the agent runtime's critic, which retries once with the reason as a hint:

| Operation | The answer must be |
|---|---|
| Tags | a JSON array (or comma list) of 1–10 short tags |
| Summary | one or two plain sentences — no headings, lists or quotes, and shorter than the note |
| Translate | not the source text back, and of a plausible length (not a fraction of the note, not three times it) |

A note whose answer still fails is counted as *failed* with its reason —
listed under "Rejected answers" in the panel — and is never written.

pages.title: Cloud only by choice
pages.description: Every AI feature has an engine on this device; a cloud service is used only when you choose it. The full list of cloud routes and what each needs.
pages.md:
Lumen's AI runs on this device by default. A cloud service is contacted
only after you choose it, and the **AI policy**
(`⌘K → "AI: Local or Cloud Policy"`) decides how far that choice goes:

| Policy | What may leave this device |
|---|---|
| **Local only** (the default on a fresh install) | Nothing. Every cloud route below is refused before a request is made; the network layer blocks it a second time and the privacy ledger lists the attempt. |
| **Local first** | Only a fallback to the AI provider whose key you entered, when no local engine can answer. Services you never set up — the public LanguageTool API, the browser's online speech recognition, server-side read-aloud voices — stay off. |
| **Cloud** | The selected provider directly, and the third-party services in the table. |

An installation that was set up with a cloud key before policies existed
starts in *local first* (with a cloud provider selected: *cloud*), so an
upgrade never silently changes where prompts go. Pick a policy once and
that choice wins.

## Every cloud route

Each route has an id; `src/__tests__/cloudRoutes.test.ts` fails when a
source file reaches a cloud service without being in this list, or when a
route loses its gate.

| Capability | Route id | On this device | Cloud option | Cloud used when |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Chat, writing, agents | `chat-openai` | Ollama, then web-llm (WebGPU) | OpenAI | provider selected; *local first* fallback |
| Chat, writing, agents | `chat-anthropic` | Ollama, then web-llm (WebGPU) | Anthropic (Claude) | provider selected; *local first* fallback |
| Chat, writing, agents | `chat-gemini` | Ollama, then web-llm (WebGPU) | Google Gemini | provider selected; *local first* fallback |
| Chat, writing, agents | `chat-mistral` | Ollama, then web-llm (WebGPU) | Mistral | provider selected; *local first* fallback |
| Smart search embeddings | `embeddings-openai` | Ollama embedding model, else multilingual-e5-small (transformers.js) | OpenAI embeddings | *cloud* only |
| Batch jobs | `batch-api` | the local batch queue | OpenAI / Anthropic Batch API | *cloud* only |
| Fine-tuning | `fine-tune` | style profiles | OpenAI fine-tuning | outside *local only*, when you run it |
| Voice memo transcription | `whisper-1` | Whisper in the browser (transformers.js) | OpenAI `whisper-1` | *cloud*; *local first* when the local model fails |
| Grammar check | `languagetool` | a LanguageTool on this machine, else the local proofreader agent | the public LanguageTool API (or a remote LanguageTool you configured) | public API: *cloud* only; your own remote server: outside *local only* |
| Web research | `web-research` | your library, or a research service on this machine | Claude web search / a hosted research service | outside *local only*, after the one-time web consent |
| Dictation | `speech-recognition` | voice memo with local Whisper | the browser's speech recognition (Chrome sends the audio to Google) | *cloud* only |
| Read aloud | `network-voices` | the system's on-device voices | server-side browser voices ("Google …") | *cloud* only |
| PlantUML diagrams | `plantuml-kroki` | — (no local renderer yet) | kroki.io draws the diagram from its text | *cloud*; otherwise only for a diagram you choose to send ("Render this diagram with kroki.io") |
| Jewish sources | `sefaria-texts` | the copy you saved for offline (Sources/Sefaria) | Sefaria's texts API: the reference only, such as "Genesis 1:1" | under any policy, each time you confirm a lookup; a saved source needs no request |

Model downloads (Hugging Face, the OCR and dictionary files) carry no
content of yours; they are listed in the privacy ledger and happen only
when a feature needs the model.

## Checking it yourself

- `⌘K → "Privacy ledger"` lists every AI request: host, size, policy and
  whether it was allowed or blocked.
- The end-to-end test `e2e/local-only-all-commands.spec.ts` runs every AI
  command under *local only* with cloud keys saved and a cloud provider
  selected, and expects zero requests to any cloud host.

pages.title: AI cost — usage meter and answer cache
pages.description: See what your AI requests cost, and avoid paying twice for the same answer.
pages.md:
Lumen calls the AI provider you choose with your own API key. Two
features keep that bill visible and small. Both run locally on your
device.

## Usage meter

Command: `AI: Usage & Cost This Month` (`⌘K`).

For the current month it lists requests, input and output tokens, and an
estimated cost per provider and model.

- **Exact counts** come from the provider whenever its API reports them:
  OpenAI, Claude (including prompt-cache reads and writes), Gemini and
  Mistral, both for regular and streamed answers.
- **Estimated counts** (about 4 characters per token) are used when the
  provider reports nothing, and are marked as estimated.
- **Local models** (Ollama, in-browser WebGPU) are counted at $0.
- **Prices** come from a built-in table of list prices, dated in the
  report. Treat them as an estimate; your provider's dashboard is the
  real bill. Models missing from the table are counted but not priced.

Usage stays in this browser's storage. It isn't synced and is never sent
anywhere.

## Answer cache

Command: `AI: Answer Cache…`.

Some commands transform a given text deterministically: auto-tag,
translate, diagram from text, action items, chart from data and heading
suggestions. When you run one of them again on exactly the same input
with the same provider and model, Lumen reuses the stored answer
instead of paying for a new one. Cache hits appear in the usage report.

- Change the text, the model or the provider and the request goes to the
  model again.
- Answers expire after 30 days. At most 500 are kept, and the oldest are
  dropped first.
- From the command you can turn the cache off (every request then asks
  the model) or clear it.
- Cached answers are stored in this browser's IndexedDB, on this device
  only.

## Claude prompt caching

With Claude, long system prompts and long documents sent as context
(about 8,000 characters or more) are marked for Anthropic's prompt cache.
A follow-up request on the same document within about five minutes reads
that prefix at roughly 10% of the normal input price. The usage report
shows these cache reads separately.

## Cost mode

Command: `AI: Cost Mode (Economy / Balanced / Quality)…`.

| Mode | Small tasks¹ | Other requests | Context per question² |
|---|---|---|---|
| Economy | Small model | Small model | ~2,000 tokens |
| Balanced (default) | Small model | Your chosen model | ~5,000 tokens |
| Quality | Your chosen model | Your chosen model | ~12,000 tokens |

¹ Tags, heading suggestions, completions and commit messages. The small
models are GPT-4o mini, Claude Haiku 5.5, Gemini 2.5 Flash and Mistral
Small. Local providers (Ollama, WebGPU) are never rerouted, and a
request that names its own model is left alone.

² **Ask Workspace** reads the matching notes in full, then sends only
the parts relevant to your question. Each note is split at its
headings, the sections are ranked against the question (BM25), and the
best ones are kept within the budget. Every note also sends its heading
outline, so the model still sees how it is structured. Notes that
already fit are sent unchanged.

## Batch over a folder (half price)

Command: `AI: Batch over a Folder (half price)…`, then `AI: Check Batch Jobs`.

To tag, summarise or translate many notes, Lumen sends them as one job to
the provider's batch API: OpenAI's Batch API or Anthropic's Message
Batches. Both charge half the normal price and return results within
24 hours.

1. Pick what to do (tags, a one-line `summary` in the front matter, or
   a translation into a new `name.<language>.md` file next to each note)
   and which folder to process.
2. Lumen shows the number of notes and an estimated cost before
   anything is sent. Each note counts as one AI prompt against your
   plan's quota.
3. Later, run `AI: Check Batch Jobs`. When a job has finished, Lumen
   shows how many notes will change and how many files will be created,
   and applies the changes only after you confirm. Notes that are open
   in a tab are skipped, and existing files are never overwritten by a
   translation.

Batch jobs need the OpenAI or Anthropic provider. Their usage appears
in the usage report at batch prices.

### Known limitations — status

| Id | Limitation | Status |
|---|---|---|
| A9 | A retry after a failure saving the job's state could write one duplicate translation | Fixed. Each translation carries its job's marker, and a retry looks for it among all `name.<language>-N.md` files of the note, so deleting a lower-numbered copy in between no longer leads to a second copy. |

pages.title: Data analyst
pages.description: Ask a question about a table in your note; a short Python program answers it on this device, checked by a second run.
pages.md:
Put a table in the note: a ```` ```csv ```` block, a Markdown table, or
comma-separated lines. Then run `⌘K → AI: Analyse the table` and ask your
question, for example "Which month had the most deaths from disease?" or
"Total sales in 2025?".

## What happens

1. **A program, not a guess.** The analyst agent writes a short Python 3
   program for the question. It may use only the standard library (`csv`,
   `statistics`, `math`, `datetime`, `json`) and receives the table as
   `inputs["csv"]`. A validator rejects a program that does not read the
   table, does not print a JSON answer, or imports anything outside that
   list (`random`, `time`, `os`, the network…).
2. **The sandbox.** The program runs in the [`run_python`](/ai/local-agents/)
   sandbox: Pyodide on this device, with no network, no workspace files and a
   time limit.
3. **A second run.** The same program runs again in a fresh sandbox. If the
   two answers differ, or either run fails, you get no answer: only the
   reason.
4. **Into the note.** The answer is added as a quote, followed by a
   ```` ```live-python ```` block that holds the table and the program. You
   can re-run it and see exactly how the number was computed. When the
   program returns chart data, a ```` ```chart ```` block is added too.

The model that writes the program is your local one (Ollama or the
in-browser model) under the AI policy, like every other agent. The table is
sent to it as text (the first 12 lines, for the column names) and nowhere
else.

## Quality

`node scripts/golden/evals/data-analysis.mjs --dev` runs the golden
questions through the same sandbox path. The target is at least 85% correct
numeric answers on 20 golden questions with a real model. That measurement
is the owner's (plan 15.13).

pages.title: DictaLM 3.0 (Hebrew)
pages.description: Dicta's Hebrew–English model in the local model catalogue — what is verified, what waits for a check, and when it may become the default.
pages.md:
[DictaLM 3.0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.02104) is Dicta's open Hebrew–English
model family, with tool calling and a 65k-token context. It comes in three
sizes, each adapted from a different base model:

| Size | Base model | Licence | In Lumen |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.7B | Qwen3-1.7B | Apache-2.0 (verified) | In the model catalogue; download it by name in *AI settings* (Ollama) as `hf.co/dicta-il/DictaLM-3.0-1.7B-Thinking-GGUF`. Never suggested by default yet |
| 12B | NVIDIA Nemotron Nano V2 | **not verified yet** | Not offered |
| 24B | Mistral-Small-3.1 | **not verified yet** | Not offered |

A model is only offered once its licence is checked in the licence gate
(`npm run licenses`). The 12B and 24B weights' licence and their exact
repositories have not been checked yet, so they are not in any list; they are
recorded in `models/registry.json` as *unknown*.

## When it becomes the default

DictaLM 3.0 replaces the Hebrew model Lumen suggests today only when it scores
**at least 5 points higher** on the agent eval and the Hebrew prompt eval,
measured on your own machine:

- 1.7B is compared with `qwen3:4b` (what Lumen suggests on a 4 GB machine).
- 12B and 24B are compared with `qwen3:14b`.

A model whose licence is a custom one (not an open licence) is offered with
its licence notice, but never becomes the default.

## Running the comparison (developers)

The sizes and their open checks are in `models/dictalm3.json`.

```sh
npm run dictalm3                         # each size, its licence and open checks
npm run dictalm3 -- eval --size 1.7B     # eval both models with Ollama → eval/results/
npm run dictalm3 -- decide --json eval/results/dictalm3-decision.json
```

`eval` refuses a size while any of its checks is open: the repository, the
commit that was evaluated, the Ollama name and the licence. `decide` prints,
for each size, *blocked*, *no results*, *keep*, *offer* or *switch*, and the
catalogue line to add to `src/ai/modelCatalog.ts` when there is one.

pages.description: One check of the whole local-AI stack, from Ollama to the on-device engines, with the exact fix for each row.
pages.md:
Open it with `⌘K → AI: Doctor (diagnose local AI)`. Each row shows what the doctor found, and
every row that is not OK also gives the fix: a command to copy, a button
that applies the fix, or a link. The checks only read state. None of them
downloads a model or sends your notes anywhere.

## What it checks

| Row | OK when | Fix when it is not |
|---|---|---|

pages.title: Hebrew dictation, models and accuracy
pages.description: Which speech model Lumen uses for Hebrew in the browser and on phones, how each sentence is re-read by Whisper, and how accuracy (WER) is measured.
pages.md:
Dictation runs on your device. The audio never leaves it.

## Which model, when

| Situation | Model | Size | Licence |
|---|---|---|---|
| Live dictation, while you speak | ivrit.ai Zipformer2, streaming (WASM) | 72 MB | CC BY 4.0 |
| Each finished sentence, on a GPU with WebGPU and f16 | ivrit.ai Whisper large-v3-turbo | ~563 MB | Apache-2.0 |
| Each finished sentence, without WebGPU or on a phone | Ozen v1 (distilled from ivrit.ai turbo) | ~164 MB | Apache-2.0 |
| A Hebrew audio file or recording | turbo on a strong GPU, otherwise Ozen v1 | | |

**Live dictation streams first, then corrects.** While you speak, the
streaming model shows text right away. When you pause, the audio of that
sentence goes through Whisper, and the result is inserted instead. That
happens only if it arrives within 2 seconds and reads as the same sentence.
Otherwise the streaming text stays, so a slow or confused second pass never
loses your words.

**Nothing is downloaded during dictation.** The second pass uses a model
only if it's already on your device. Transcribe one Hebrew file to get it:
turbo on a capable GPU, Ozen v1 everywhere else. Without WebGPU, Ozen runs
on WebAssembly, which works on phones too.

Why Ozen v1 replaced whisper-base for Hebrew: its model card reports 8.6%
WER against 48% for whisper-base on ivrit.ai's podcast set (eval-d1), at
about the same size.

## How accuracy is measured

WER (word error rate) is measured on **FLEURS-he validation**, the set
where the streaming model scores 23.6%. The target is **15% or less**.

```sh
npm run eval:asr-web -- --fleurs <folder from scripts/asr/fleurs_spike.py>
```

This runs the same ONNX files and settings the browser uses. It's also one
step of `npm run models:day`.

The report gives two normal forms, side by side:

- **v1**: no niqqud, no punctuation, maqaf splits words, lower case.
- **v2**: v1, plus numbers count the same whether written as words or
  digits ("אלפיים ועשרים" = "2020"), "%" equals the word "אחוז", and a
  one-letter prefix on a number is its own word ("ב2020" = "ב 2020").
  Latin words are **not** transliterated ("Google" ≠ "גוגל"). That error
  stays in the score.

v2 is the headline number. v1 stays next to it, so it can be compared
with earlier runs.

pages.description: Alt text for pasted and attached images — OCR, a local vision model, or a captioning model in the browser. Nothing is sent to the cloud.
pages.md:
An image with no alt text, or with only its file name (`IMG_1234`,
`Screenshot 2026-…`), gets a real description. Lumen tries, in order:

1. **OCR** — an image that is mostly text (a screenshot, a slide, a scan)
   gets that text: the first line as alt text, the full text as the image
   title, so search finds it.
2. **A vision model in Ollama** on this machine (qwen2.5vl, gemma3, llava,
   moondream…), asked for one sentence in the note's language.
3. **A captioning model in the browser** — Florence-2 base-ft (Microsoft,
   MIT, ≈ 224 MB), with SmolVLM-256M-Instruct (Hugging Face, Apache-2.0,
   ≈ 189 MB) when Florence-2 cannot load on this device or gives nothing
   usable. Both run in a background worker (WebGPU when available) and
   describe in English; the description is then translated into the note's
   language with [local translation](/ai/translation/). When no local
   translation can take the pair, the English description is kept.
4. Otherwise the file name stays. Lumen never invents alt text.

Every description is checked before it is written: not empty, at least two
words, not the file name or a camera placeholder, not the prompt read back.

## Downloads

The browser models are downloaded from Hugging Face only after you agree
in a dialog that shows the model, its size, its licence and its
attribution. That dialog appears only when you run
`⌘K → Images: alt text from OCR / local vision`. Pasting an image never
asks; it uses a browser model only after you agreed to it once from the
command. Declining stops there: Lumen does not offer the fallback model
in the same run.

To turn off automatic alt text for pasted images, set
`lumen.ai.imageText` to `off`.

## Measured

| Check | Status |
|---|---|
| Order, consent, fallback, validator, translation | unit tests (`caption.test.ts`, `captionWorker.test.ts`) |
| Quality: ≥ 80% of the 50 images of the caption golden set rated ≥ 4 / 5 | **not measured yet** — the set's Crossmodal-3600 part is built by the golden-sets workflow and the other 20 images and all ratings are the owner's (plan 15.11, 15.15) |
| Speed and memory on real hardware | not measured: the models are not reachable from the build machine |

pages.title: Image search by description
pages.description: Find an image in your notes by describing it, in Hebrew or English, on this device.
pages.md:
Open the search dialog (`⌘⇧F`), switch to **Images** and describe the
picture: "a red bicycle by the sea", "צילום מסך של הגדרות". Lumen
ranks the vault's images by how well each one matches the description and
shows them as thumbnails. Click an image to copy its Markdown link, then
paste it into the note.

## How it works

- **Model.** SigLIP base multilingual (Google, Apache-2.0). Lumen converts
  it to ONNX itself (plan 6.0) and serves it from its own host. It runs in
  the transformers.js worker, on WebGPU when the browser has it and on
  WebAssembly otherwise.
- **Consent.** The first search asks before downloading the model and shows
  its size, licence and attribution. The model is verified against the
  registry's checksums and cached on this device.
- **Indexing.** Each image is embedded once. Later searches embed only
  images that are new or changed (size or modification time), and drop
  deleted ones. The vectors are kept in this browser's IndexedDB.
- **Hebrew.** SigLIP's Hebrew quality has not been measured on the
  image-search golden set yet. Until it is, a Hebrew description is first
  translated to English on this device by [local translation](/ai/translation/),
  using only layers that are already available, with no second download
  prompt. The tab shows the English it searched with. If no local layer can
  translate, the Hebrew is used as written.
- **Privacy.** Images, descriptions and vectors stay on this device.

## Availability

The converted models need a host, which the owner has not chosen yet (plan
15.9). Until then the tab explains that the model can't be downloaded yet,
and nothing is fetched.

## Quality

`node scripts/golden/evals/image-search.mjs --dev --models <dir>` measures
recall@1, recall@5 and nDCG@10 per query language on the image-search
golden set. The target is recall@5 ≥ 80% for Hebrew queries.

pages.title: Local agents
pages.description: Every AI command runs through one local agent runtime — the model proposes, tools execute, validators decide, and an improvement agent steps in when there is no answer.
pages.md:
Lumen's AI commands are **agents**: a definition of what to ask the
model, which tools it may call, what shape the answer must have and how
to check it. One runtime (`src/agents/runtime.ts`) runs every definition
against the first available **executor**, on this device whenever it
can:

| Executor | Where it runs | Tool calling | JSON output |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ollama | a local Ollama server | native (`tools`) | native (`format`) |
| web-llm | your browser, on the GPU | JSON-ReAct protocol | JSON mode |
| `chat()` | whatever provider you selected | JSON-ReAct protocol | prompt |

The **AI policy** (`⌘K → "AI: Local or Cloud Policy"`) decides whether a
cloud provider may ever be contacted. The default on a fresh install is
*local only*.

## What a run does

1. Picks the first available executor in the agent's preference order.
2. Sends the system and user prompts. When the agent has tools and the
   executor cannot call them natively, the prompt teaches the JSON-ReAct
   protocol: the model answers `{"tool": …, "args": …}` or
   `{"final": …}`, one JSON object per turn.
3. Executes each tool call. The arguments are checked against the tool's
   JSON Schema first. Tools that write or reach the network need a
   permission the command grants explicitly, and even then a write tool
   only **proposes** a change you approve, and a network tool goes out
   only when the AI policy or your consent allows it (see
   [Tools](#tools)).
4. Parses the final answer (JSON when the agent declares a schema) and
   runs the agent's **validators** — a Mermaid diagram must compile, an
   ECharts option needs series and axes, tags must exist, offsets must
   fall inside the text.
5. When there is no usable answer, the **improvement agent** (the
   critic) diagnoses the failure and proposes one change for a retry —
   temperature 0 with the validator's error fed back, then a larger
   model tier — up to two retries. If that still fails, the run ends
   with **suggestions** you can act on: start Ollama, allow the app's
   origin (`OLLAMA_ORIGINS`), pull a model, split the document, try
   another executor, or allow the cloud.
6. When the retries are used up, a small local model (the tiny tier)
   reads the failure. It may add one or two suggestions in plain
   language, and when a new attempt can fix the answer (the wrong format,
   language or length), it gives one more instruction. The runtime then
   makes **one more attempt** with that instruction.
7. The suggestions panel opens on its own. This happens for every AI
   command, including research, batch jobs, workspace search, chart
   blocks and the WYSIWYG writer. Pressing a suggestion does it, then
   runs the command again:

| Suggestion | What pressing it does |
|---|---|
| Start Ollama | Checks every two seconds whether Ollama answers. When it does, the command runs again; it gives up after two minutes, and closing the panel stops it. |
| Split the document | Runs the agent on parts of about 4000 characters and merges the answers. This is offered for agents whose answer for a part means the same as for the whole: tags, action items, translation, proofreading, links. |
| Select a part | Shown for agents whose answer can't be split, such as a diagram or an outline. Select the part you want and run the command again. |
| Download the model | Pulls the model into Ollama, or loads it in the browser. |
| Try again with … | Runs the command again with another executor or a larger model tier. |
| Allow the cloud as a fallback | Sets the AI policy to *local first*. |
| Add your key | Opens *AI: Switch Provider*. |

### "Not good"

After a command that puts one answer into your note (action items,
translation, diagram, chart, tags, links, outline, grammar, research,
style profile, commit message), a small **Not good — try again** button
appears for a few seconds. Pressing it runs the command again on the
same input, at a higher temperature and one model tier up, and the
model is told which answer was rejected. In the agent trace, the new
run is linked to the run it replaces (`retryOf`).

Every run is recorded on this device: `⌘K → "AI: Recent Agent Runs"`
shows the executor, model, tool calls, retries and failures of the last
50 runs.

## Tools

Every tool declares a JSON Schema for its arguments and a scope. The
runtime refuses a call whose arguments do not match (numbers and
booleans sent as strings are accepted), and every call — with its
outcome — is in the run's trace.

| Scope | Tools | What the runtime does |
|---|---|---|
| read | `read_file`, `list_files`, `file_exists`, `search_workspace`, `get_frontmatter`, `list_tags`, `get_document`, `get_selection`, `get_headings`, `validate_mermaid`, `validate_echarts`, `validate_json`, `git_diff`, `extract_quotes`, `csv_parse`, `run_python` | Always allowed. |
| write | `write_file`, `set_frontmatter`, `replace_range` | Needs the run's `write` grant. The tool never writes: it **stages** the change (`src/agents/staging.ts`) and the run lists the staged ids. Only approving a change writes it — and only if the file or the text it was computed from has not changed since; otherwise it is marked as a conflict. A cancelled run withdraws what it staged. |
| network | `search_web`, `fetch_page` | Needs the run's `network` grant. Both go through the research service (a local SearXNG or the research worker) — never a direct request to a web page — and send only the query or the page address. The agent writes that query itself, possibly from your notes, so text from them can be in it. Under **local only** every call asks you first: the prompt names the tool, the host and shows exactly what is sent, all of it, and the call then goes out with exactly the service and settings it named, and a one-time consent you gave to web research does not count for agents. Without your yes the call is refused before anything is sent, and the refusal is recorded. Every request is recorded in the privacy ledger, marked when it went out on consent. |

`git_diff` shows the unified diff of a cloned repository: HEAD against
the working copy by default (what the next commit records), or against
the index with `staged`. `set_frontmatter` edits YAML frontmatter
through the `yaml` document model, so comments and the other keys stay
as they were. `extract_quotes` checks quotes word for word against a
page read in the same run, a workspace file or the open document, and
returns the exact text with its offsets. All tools stop when the run is
cancelled.

## Reviewing proposed changes

When an agent proposes changes, a toast says so and the status bar shows
**Review N**; `⌘K → "AI: Review changes proposed by agents"` opens the
same panel. Each change is shown as a diff — a whole file line by line,
a part of the open document word by word, marked like a tracked change —
with the agent and the run that proposed it. Approve or reject each one,
or all of them at once; nothing is written before you approve.

- A change to a document that is open (saved or not) goes into its text
  in the editor, not into the file underneath, and saving writes it. In
  the source editor Undo takes it back; in Preview or WYSIWYG it can't,
  and the panel says so. Changes to other files are written to the
  workspace.
- A change to a document that isn't in the workspace (an untitled or
  imported one) only ever goes to the document the agent worked on, even
  after you switch tabs; if that document was closed, the change is
  refused.
- With **suggesting mode** on, an approved change is added as a tracked
  change attributed to the agent (`{~~old~>new~~}{>>@AI proofreader<<}`),
  so you can still accept or reject it in place.
- If the text a change replaces was edited after the proposal, the
  change is refused and the panel says why; when the replaced text only
  moved, and appears exactly once, it is applied where it is now.
  Several changes from one run can be approved in any order.
- Cancelling a run withdraws the changes it proposed.

### Which agent uses which tools

| Agent | Tools |
|---|---|
| tagger | `list_tags` |
| linker | `list_files`, `search_workspace` |
| outliner | `get_document`, `get_headings` |
| tasker, translator, proofreader | `get_document` |
| diagrammer | `validate_mermaid` |
| charter | `csv_parse`, `validate_echarts` |
| committer | `git_diff` (subject and a short body) |
| writer, templater | `get_selection` |
| builder | `list_files` |
| stylist | `list_files`, `read_file` |
| researcher | `search_web`, `fetch_page`, `extract_quotes`, `search_workspace`, `read_file` |

What an agent always needs — the workspace's tags for the tagger, the
note list for the linker, the parsed table for the charter, the diff
for the committer — the runtime fetches through the same tool path
before the model starts, so the model sees it as its own call and can
ask for more. The daily digest reads the vault the same way.

On a small model, every turn is held to a JSON Schema (Ollama's
`format`, web-llm's grammar): a call to one of the agent's own tools
with valid arguments, or the final answer in the agent's format. A
streaming agent (writer, templater) gets its tools' results before it
starts, and its answer still streams.

The builder writes the whole project at once, when every file is done:
if one fails, none is written.

### Outside content (prompt injection)

Web pages, search results, clipped pages (the `Library` / `ספרייה`
folder or a `source: https://…` frontmatter), notes that came from a git
clone or pull, notes with `untrusted: true` in their frontmatter, and the
notes that Research writes (they carry that frontmatter, because they are
built from pages and quotes) are **outside content**. Someone else wrote them, and they may contain
instructions planted for the agent. The runtime (`src/agents/untrusted.ts`)
handles them like this:

- **Delimited.** The model gets such text between `⟪untrusted id=…⟫` and
  `⟪/untrusted id=…⟫` markers. The id is random, so the content cannot
  close the block itself. The system prompt says that text inside the
  markers is data and never instructions.
- **Cleaned, never silently.** Unicode tag characters (invisible ASCII)
  are decoded and shown. Zero-width characters and bidi controls are
  removed, and their count is printed on the block. HTML comments and
  CSS-hidden elements are shown as hidden. Instruction-like passages in
  English and Hebrew ("ignore previous instructions", "התעלם מכל
  ההוראות", role tokens, "send this note to …") stay in the text inside
  a visible `⟦flagged …⟧` marker.
- **Approval.** Once a run has outside content in its context, every
  write tool and every network call asks you first. The prompt names the
  tool, what it would do and where the outside content came from. Under
  **local only**, a network call's own prompt carries the same warning.
  Without your yes nothing is staged or sent. Approving a staged change
  is still a separate step. For a git repository you own you can turn the
  write question off: see [Trusted repositories](/security/trusted-repos/).

The rules are deterministic, so they work the same in Hebrew and English
and need no model. They do not catch a politely worded request ("please
also save a copy as …"). The approval step is what stops those. An
optional English classifier (ProtectAI v2) for the desktop app is a
follow-up.

### `run_python`: Python on this device, offline

`run_python` runs a short Python 3 program on the same self-hosted
Pyodide as the `live-python` block (the standard library, without the
modules Pyodide ships as separate packages, such as `ssl`, `sqlite3` and
`lzma`, and without third-party packages) and returns
what it printed (`stdout`, `stderr`), the value of its last expression
(`result`) or the error, with the Pyodide frames removed from the
traceback. It is a **read** tool, and it makes no requests at all, so it
needs no grant and asks no network consent:

- It runs in a Web Worker made for that one call and terminated after
  it, so nothing carries over from one call to the next. The worker has
  no DOM, and no way to reach your vault: IndexedDB, Cache Storage,
  `navigator.storage` (OPFS), `navigator.storageBuckets` and
  `BroadcastChannel` are removed before
  the code runs, and so are the device APIs (`navigator.serial`, `usb`,
  `hid`, `bluetooth`, `geolocation`, `mediaDevices`). If the code needs a note, the agent passes the text in
  `inputs` (a JSON object of at most 64 KB, which the code reads as the
  dict `inputs`).
- There is no network. Once Pyodide has loaded its own files (from this
  site, under `/pyodide/`), the worker replaces `fetch`, `XMLHttpRequest`,
  `WebSocket`, `EventSource`, `importScripts`, nested workers and the rest
  with stubs that fail, on the worker's global object and on its
  prototypes. It also refuses JavaScript built from strings (`eval`, the
  `Function` constructors, `setTimeout` with a string). In Python, an
  audit hook refuses sockets and `urllib` requests, and `pyodide.http`
  (`pyfetch`, `open_url`, `pyxhr`), `pyodide.code.run_js`, `micropip` and
  `pyodide_js.loadPackage` fail. Each attempt is recorded in the
  privacy ledger as blocked, with the host only
  (up to 20 entries per call).

  starting once Pyodide is up), after which the worker is stopped and
  the result says `timedOut`. Output (stdout, stderr and the value
  together) is capped at 20,000 characters, with `truncated` set. The
  code itself can be up to 20,000 characters. Cancelling the run stops

works offline once the app is cached). Each call starts it again.

### Every AI command is an agent

All AI commands run through the agent runtime: the executors (local first), the AI policy, the quota, the injection guard and the trace. That includes the ones that used to call the model directly: ghost text and the inline suggestion (`completer`), AI Rewrite (`rewriter`, which also follows your style profile), Ask Workspace (`answerer`), the voice-memo summary (`memo-summarizer`), the builder's architecture / tests / README stages, and batch jobs (`batch`, on the job's local model, charged once when the job is submitted). A test checks the source: nothing outside the executors calls the model directly.

## AI settings

`⌘K → "AI: Settings (local agents)"` gathers everything in one panel:

- the AI policy;
- **who runs the agents** — automatic (Ollama → browser → chat provider)
  or one executor first, with a live *available / not available* check
  for each;
- the Ollama address and model, with the models already installed;
- the in-browser model, the device card (WebGPU, f16, a VRAM budget
  estimate) and the catalogue, with models too large for this device
  disabled;
- the grammar (LanguageTool) and research (SearXNG worker) addresses;
- your writing-style profile on/off;
- the last ten agent runs.

The panel writes the same settings the runtime reads; nothing is stored
twice. The VRAM budget is a heuristic from the browser's coarse hints,
not a measurement.

## Model manager

The same panel manages the models themselves:

- **AI mode** — *economy*, *balanced* (the default) or *quality*. For the
  local executors it moves the model tier of the next agent run: economy
  runs one size smaller than the agent asks for (a tagger that wants a
  *small* model gets a *tiny* one), quality one size larger, balanced as
  declared. The device budget still applies, so *quality* on a 4 GB
  machine gets the largest model that fits, not a larger one. A run that
  is already going keeps its model; a retry that climbs a tier climbs
  from the mode's tier. The cloud chat provider keeps its own routing
  (see [Cost](/ai/cost/)); the mode also sets how much of your notes is
  sent as context.

  | Agent tier | Economy | Balanced | Quality |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | tiny | tiny | tiny | small |
  | small | tiny | small | medium |
  | medium | small | medium | large |
  | large | medium | large | large |

  The mode moves the *automatic* choice. A model you picked yourself
  wins: an in-browser model chosen in the panel runs whenever it is at
  least the tier asked for (pick *Recommended for this device* to let the
  mode choose), and a configured Ollama model runs when it fits the
  tier.

  Ollama tiers are by parameter count (tiny ≤ 2.5 B, small ≤ 9 B,
  medium ≤ 16 B, larger is large) among the models you have installed;
  web-llm tiers are the catalogue's.
- **Download an Ollama model** — type a name (`qwen3:4b`,
  `hf.co/<owner>/<repo>`) and *Download*: the panel streams Ollama's
  `/api/pull` and shows the progress over all layers in bytes and
  percent, with *Cancel*. An edited address is saved first. A model under
  its own licence (Llama, Gemma, non-commercial ones) is named and
  confirmed before the download. When it finishes the installed list refreshes.
  The download goes to the Ollama server at the address above; no note
  content is involved.
- **Storage** — how much this site uses of the browser's quota
  (`navigator.storage.estimate()`), and two buttons: *Clear in-browser
  models* removes web-llm's caches (`webllm/model`, `webllm/wasm`,
  `webllm/config`, in Cache Storage or IndexedDB) after unloading the
  model, and *Clear speech and search models* removes transformers.js's
  cache (Whisper, embeddings). The app's own offline cache and your vault
  are not touched. The next use downloads the model again.
- **No WebGPU** — Firefox has no WebGPU on Linux and Android yet, and
  Android browsers vary. The panel says so by name: the in-browser chat
  model is off there, speech and search models run on WASM (slower,
  smaller models), and agents use Ollama (or the chat provider, if the
  policy allows it).

## Transcription and embeddings on this device

Speech recognition and text embeddings do not go through a chat model:
they run in a second worker on
[transformers.js](https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.js) with
ONNX Runtime (WebGPU when the GPU is usable, wasm otherwise). The ONNX
Runtime files are served from this app's own origin (`/ort/`), so no CDN
is contacted; the models come from Hugging Face and are cached in the
browser.

| Task | Model | Size | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Voice memo (`🎙 Voice memo`) | `onnx-community/whisper-small` | ≈ 250 MB | WebGPU; multilingual (Hebrew included) |
| Voice memo on a strong GPU | `onnx-community/whisper-large-v3-turbo` | ≈ 800 MB | WebGPU, ≥ 6 GB budget |
| Voice memo without WebGPU | `onnx-community/whisper-tiny` | ≈ 40 MB | wasm, slower |
| Smart search embeddings | `Xenova/multilingual-e5-small` | ≈ 120 MB | 384 dimensions, ~100 languages |

Under *local only* the cloud Whisper API is never used; under *local
first* it is the fallback when the local path fails; under *cloud* it is
used directly.

## Ollama from the hosted app

A page served from `https://lumen-md.vercel.app` may only call your
local Ollama when Ollama allows that origin:

```
OLLAMA_ORIGINS=https://lumen-md.vercel.app ollama serve
```

(on macOS: `launchctl setenv OLLAMA_ORIGINS https://lumen-md.vercel.app`
and restart Ollama). Without it Ollama answers `403` and the improvement
agent suggests exactly this fix. The desktop app and `localhost`
development builds need no change.

## Research, grammar and search on this machine

`docker/local-ai.yml` starts three services:

| Service | Port | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| SearXNG | 8888 | Metasearch, no API key |
| research service | 8787 | The same worker Lumen deploys (`edge-workers/research`), run with `wrangler dev`: page extraction plus SearXNG search |
| LanguageTool | 8010 | Grammar and spelling checks |

```
export RESEARCH_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 24)
echo "$RESEARCH_TOKEN"
docker compose -f docker/local-ai.yml up -d
```

The research service requires a shared token. Copy the value printed by
`echo` into AI settings → Research token (keep it: later `docker compose`
runs need the same `RESEARCH_TOKEN`). Then `⌘K → Research: Settings → SearXNG on
this machine` and enter `http://localhost:8787`. Research questions are planned and answered by
your local model; quotes are still verified word for word against the
pages. Under *local only* a research service off this machine or network
is refused. On a fresh install with the *local only* policy, SearXNG is
the default research provider.

## Evaluating a local model

`npm run eval:agents` runs the fixed eval cases — at least five for each
of the 14 agents, in Hebrew and English — through the real agent runtime
against your Ollama, and writes a Markdown, JSON and HTML report to
`eval/results/`. The cases, the checks and how to read the report are on
[Agent eval](/ai/agent-eval/).

```bash
ollama pull qwen2.5:7b
npm run eval:agents -- --model qwen2.5:7b
npm run eval:agents -- --model llama3.1:8b --only tagger-he,tasker-he
```

In CI the same cases run against a **fake Ollama server**
(`npm run fake-ollama`, `scripts/fake-ollama.mjs`) over real HTTP: the
runtime, the Ollama executor, the parsers and validators are exercised on
every pull request without a GPU. Only model quality needs the live run.

Every check is deterministic (Hebrew share of the letters, required and
forbidden words, list lengths, length limits, a pattern), so two models
or two prompt versions can be compared on the same numbers. The report
lists each case with pass/fail, attempts (retries the improvement agent
asked for) and time. The reference answers in
`src/agents/eval/fixtures.ts` run in CI through each agent's own parser
and validators, so a broken fixture is caught before a long GPU run.

### A real tiny model in CI

`npm run ci:real-model` runs every agent once against a real local model, `qwen3:0.6b` on Ollama (Apache-2.0, about 523 MB, tool calling). Each run uses temperature 0, seed 42, no thinking phase, and at most 64 tokens a turn. It judges the **shape** of each turn, not its wording:
- a tool call names one of the agent's tools, and its arguments pass the tool's JSON Schema;
- a final answer starts in the agent's format (JSON where the agent has a schema).

It finds Ollama, or starts `ollama serve` if the binary is installed, and pulls the model when it is missing. If either is impossible (no Ollama, no network to the model registry), it writes `eval/results/real-skipped.md` with the reason and exits 0. The nightly workflow (`.github/workflows/real-model.yml`) caches the model and sets `LUMEN_REAL_MODEL_REQUIRED=1`, so there a skip fails. It also checks LanguageTool (English only; it has no Hebrew) and SearXNG as real services. Use `--model qwen3:1.7b` for the multi-step scenarios.

One runtime (src/agents/runtime.ts) runs every definition against the first available executor , on this device whenever it can: Executor Where it runs Tool calling JSON output --- --- --- --- Ollama a local Ollama server native (tools) native (format) web-llm your browser, on the GPU JSON-ReAct protocol JSON mode chat() whatever provider you selected JSON-ReAct protocol prompt The AI policy (⌘K → "AI: Local or Cloud Policy") decides whether a cloud provider may ever be contacted. sections.heading: What a run does
sections.text: 1. Picks the first available executor in the agent's preference order. 2. Sends the system and user prompts. When the agent has tools and the executor cannot call them natively, the prompt teaches the JSON-ReAct protocol: the model answers {"tool": …, "args": …} or {"final": …}, one JSON object per turn. 3. Executes each tool call. The arguments are checked against the tool's JSON Schema first. Tools that write or reach the network need a permission the command grants explicitly, and even then a write tool only proposes a change you approve, and a network tool goes out only when the AI policy or your consent allows it (see Tools). 4. Parses the final answer (JSON when the agent declares a schema) and runs the agent's validators — a Mermaid diagram must compile, an ECharts option needs series and axes, tags must exist, offsets must fall inside the text. 5. When there is no usable answer, the improvement agent (the critic) diagnoses the failure and proposes one change for a retry — temperature 0 with the validator's error fed back, then a larger model tier — up to two retries. If that still fails, the run ends with suggestions you can act on: start Ollama, allow the app's origin (OLLAMA ORIGINS), pull a model, split the document, try another executor, or allow the cloud. 6. When the retries are used up, a small local model (the tiny tier) reads the failure. It may add one or two suggestions in plain language, and when a new attempt can fix the answer (the wrong format, language or length), it gives one more instruction. The runtime then makes one more attempt with that instruction. 7. The suggestions panel opens on its own. This happens for every AI command, including research, batch jobs, workspace search, chart blocks and the WYSIWYG writer. Pressing a suggestion does it, then runs the command again: Suggestion What pressing it does --- --- Start Ollama Checks every two seconds whether Ollama answers. When it does, the command runs again; it gives up after two minutes, and closing the panel stops it. Split the document Runs the agent on parts of about 4000 characters and merges the answers. This is offered for agents whose answer for a part means the same as for the whole: tags, action items, translation, proofreading, links. Select a part Shown for agents whose answer can't be split, such as a diagram or an outline. Select the part you want and run the command again. Download the model Pulls the model into Ollama, or loads it in the browser. Try again with … Runs the command again with another executor or a larger model tier. Allow the cloud as a fallback Sets the AI policy to local first . Add your key Opens AI: Switch Provider .

sections.heading: "Not good"
sections.text: After a command that puts one answer into your note (action items, translation, diagram, chart, tags, links, outline, grammar, research, style profile, commit message), a small Not good — try again button appears for a few seconds. Pressing it runs the command again on the same input, at a higher temperature and one model tier up, and the model is told which answer was rejected. In the agent trace, the new run is linked to the run it replaces (retryOf). Every run is recorded on this device: ⌘K → "AI: Recent Agent Runs" shows the executor, model, tool calls, retries and failures of the last 50 runs.

sections.heading: Tools
sections.text: Every tool declares a JSON Schema for its arguments and a scope. The runtime refuses a call whose arguments do not match (numbers and booleans sent as strings are accepted), and every call — with its outcome — is in the run's trace. Scope Tools What the runtime does --- --- --- read read file, list files, file exists, search workspace, get frontmatter, list tags, get document, get selection, get headings, validate mermaid, validate echarts, validate json, git diff, extract quotes, csv parse, run python Always allowed. write write file, set frontmatter, replace range Needs the run's write grant. The tool never writes: it stages the change (src/agents/staging.ts) and the run lists the staged ids. Only approving a change writes it — and only if the file or the text it was computed from has not changed since; otherwise it is marked as a conflict. A cancelled run withdraws what it staged. network search web, fetch page Needs the run's network grant. Both go through the research service (a local SearXNG or the research worker) — never a direct request to a web page — and send only the query or the page address. The agent writes that query itself, possibly from your notes, so text from them can be in it. Under local only every call asks you first: the prompt names the tool, the host and shows exactly what is sent, all of it, and the call then goes out with exactly the service and settings it named, and a one-time consent you gave to web research does not count for agents. Without your yes the call is refused before anything is sent, and the refusal is recorded. Every request is recorded in the privacy ledger, marked when it went out on consent. git diff shows the unified diff of a cloned repository: HEAD against the working copy by default (what the next commit records), or against the index with staged. set frontmatter edits YAML frontmatter through the yaml document model, so comments and the other keys stay as they were. extract quotes checks quotes word for word against a page read in the same run, a workspace file or the open document, and returns the exact text with its offsets. All tools stop when the run is cancelled.

sections.heading: Reviewing proposed changes
sections.text: When an agent proposes changes, a toast says so and the status bar shows Review N ; ⌘K → "AI: Review changes proposed by agents" opens the same panel. Each change is shown as a diff — a whole file line by line, a part of the open document word by word, marked like a tracked change — with the agent and the run that proposed it. Approve or reject each one, or all of them at once; nothing is written before you approve. A change to a document that is open (saved or not) goes into its text in the editor, not into the file underneath, and saving writes it. In the source editor Undo takes it back; in Preview or WYSIWYG it can't, and the panel says so. Changes to other files are written to the workspace. A change to a document that isn't in the workspace (an untitled or imported one) only ever goes to the document the agent worked on, even after you switch tabs; if that document was closed, the change is refused. With suggesting mode on, an approved change is added as a tracked change attributed to the agent ({ old >new }{>>@AI proofreader<<}), so you can still accept or reject it in place. If the text a change replaces was edited after the proposal, the change is refused and the panel says why; when the replaced text only moved, and appears exactly once, it is applied where it is now. Several changes from one run can be approved in any order. Cancelling a run withdraws the changes it proposed.

sections.heading: Outside content (prompt injection)
sections.text: Web pages, search results, clipped pages (the Library / ספרייה folder or a source: https://… frontmatter), notes that came from a git clone or pull, notes with untrusted: true in their frontmatter, and the notes that Research writes (they carry that frontmatter, because they are built from pages and quotes) are outside content . Someone else wrote them, and they may contain instructions planted for the agent. The runtime (src/agents/untrusted.ts) handles them like this: Delimited. The model gets such text between ⟪untrusted id=…⟫ and ⟪/untrusted id=…⟫ markers. The id is random, so the content cannot close the block itself. The system prompt says that text inside the markers is data and never instructions. Cleaned, never silently. Unicode tag characters (invisible ASCII) are decoded and shown. Zero-width characters and bidi controls are removed, and their count is printed on the block. HTML comments and CSS-hidden elements are shown as hidden. Instruction-like passages in English and Hebrew ("ignore previous instructions", "התעלם מכל ההוראות", role tokens, "send this note to …") stay in the text inside a visible ⟦flagged …⟧ marker. Approval. Once a run has outside content in its context, every write tool and every network call asks you first. The prompt names the tool, what it would do and where the outside content came from. Under local only , a network call's own prompt carries the same warning. Without your yes nothing is staged or sent. Approving a staged change is still a separate step. For a git repository you own you can turn the write question off: see Trusted repositories. The rules are deterministic, so they work the same in Hebrew and English and need no model. They do not catch a politely worded request ("please also save a copy as …"). The approval step is what stops those. An optional English classifier (ProtectAI v2) for the desktop app is a follow-up.

The report lists each case with pass/fail, attempts (retries the improvement agent asked for) and time. sections.heading: A real tiny model in CI
sections.text: npm run ci:real-model runs every agent once against a real local model, qwen3:0.6b on Ollama (Apache-2.0, about 523 MB, tool calling). Each run uses temperature 0, seed 42, no thinking phase, and at most 64 tokens a turn. It judges the shape of each turn, not its wording: a tool call names one of the agent's tools, and its arguments pass the tool's JSON Schema; a final answer starts in the agent's format (JSON where the agent has a schema). It finds Ollama, or starts ollama serve if the binary is installed, and pulls the model when it is missing. If either is impossible (no Ollama, no network to the model registry), it writes eval/results/real-skipped.md with the reason and exits 0. The nightly workflow (.github/workflows/real-model.yml) caches the model and sets LUMEN REAL MODEL REQUIRED=1, so there a skip fails. It also checks LanguageTool (English only; it has no Hebrew) and SearXNG as real services. Use --model qwen3:1.7b for the multi-step scenarios.

pages.md:
`⌘K → AI fine-tune settings…` now offers the **local route first**. Lumen
exports your notes as training data together with a script. You run the
script on your own computer, and the result appears in Ollama as the model
`lumen-style`. The cloud fine-tune (OpenAI) is still offered below it.

## Steps

1. Choose the notes to learn from (a folder, or all of them) and your
   computer type, then click **Export training data and script**. You get
   `lumen-lora.zip`, which contains:
   - `train.jsonl` and `valid.jsonl`: chat-format samples cut from the
     prose of your notes. Frontmatter, code and tables are left out. When
     you have a [style profile](/ai/agents/), its tone and rules go into
     the system prompt.
   - `heldout.json`: about one note in ten, which is never trained on. It
     is used to check the result.
   - `train-mac.sh` or `train-nvidia.sh`.
2. Unzip the file and run the script in its folder.
   - **Mac (Apple silicon):** the script runs `mlx_lm.lora` on Mistral 7B
     Instruct (Apache-2.0), then `mlx_lm.fuse --export-gguf`, and creates a
     Modelfile with `FROM` the GGUF. MLX can export GGUF only for Llama,
     Mistral and Mixtral, which is why the base model is Mistral.
   - **NVIDIA:** the script trains with PEFT through the Unsloth core
     library (Apache-2.0). It does not use Unsloth Studio, which is AGPL.
     It then converts the adapter with llama.cpp's `convert_lora_to_gguf.py`
     and creates a Modelfile with `ADAPTER`.
3. Select `lumen-style` as the Ollama model in the AI settings.

## Is it closer to your style?

```bash
node scripts/lora/style-eval.mjs --heldout heldout.json --base mistral:7b-instruct --tuned lumen-style
```

Both models continue the opening of each held-out note. The script embeds
the continuations and the held-out notes with your local embedding model
(`nomic-embed-text` by default) and compares the mean cosine to the
held-out notes. The target is a gain of at least 10% over the base model.
Everything runs against your local Ollama.

pages.title: Local LLM (web-llm + WebGPU)
pages.description: Run AI prompts entirely on your device — private, offline-capable, no per-token cost.
pages.md:
Lumen routes every AI command through `chat()`. With `useLocalAi`
toggled on (and a WebGPU-capable browser), prompts go to a model
running in your tab via [web-llm](https://github.com/mlc-ai/web-llm) —
nothing leaves the machine.

## Switch on

```
⌘K → "Switch to local AI (WebGPU)"
```

The first prompt downloads a model **sized for this device** — the
model manager probes the GPU (WebGPU, `shader-f16`, device memory) and
picks the largest model of the task's tier that fits, from about 0.4 GB
(SmolLM2 360M) to 6 GB (Qwen3 8B, Gemma 2 9B). Pick one yourself with
`⌘K → "AI: Local Models (WebGPU)"`, which also shows what is already
downloaded and lets you download a model ahead of time. Weights are
cached in the browser; later prompts start instantly.

Inference runs in a **Web Worker**, so the editor stays responsive
while a model loads or generates, and a toast reports download progress
at 5 % intervals.

Firefox on Linux and Android browsers have no WebGPU yet: there the
in-browser model is off and the AI settings say so; use Ollama instead.
The settings also show how much browser storage the models take and
clear it (see [Model manager](/ai/local-agents/#model-manager)).

## When to use it

- You're on a plane / café / corporate network without API access.
- The note contains secrets you don't want to put into a hosted LLM.
- You want predictable cost — local inference is free after the
  one-time download.

## When not to use it

- Long-context tasks (>4k tokens) — the 8B model loses coherence.
- Latency-sensitive flows — local inference is ≈ 5–10× slower than
  GPT-4o-mini for the first token.
- Older laptops — the model needs ≥ 4 GB of GPU memory.

## How to fall back

What happens when WebGPU (or Ollama) isn't available depends on your
**AI policy** (`⌘K → "AI: Local or Cloud Policy"`):

- **Local only** (the default on a fresh install): nothing leaves the
  device. The command stops with a clear message and the agent's
  suggestions (start Ollama, pick a smaller model, use a WebGPU browser).
- **Local first**: a reachable Ollama server answers first (also when a
  cloud provider is selected); in-browser WebGPU takes the request when
  Privacy Mode is on; only then the cloud provider with your key. An
  installation that had only a cloud key before policies existed keeps
  this behaviour until you choose.
- **Cloud**: the selected cloud provider is used directly. An
  installation that had a cloud provider selected before policies
  existed starts here.

Under **Local only** every other path that would send content to a third
party stops as well: smart-search embeddings, Whisper transcription,
batch jobs, fine-tuning, Claude web search, a remote research service and
the public LanguageTool API (a LanguageTool or SearXNG on this machine or
network is fine).

See [Local agents](/ai/local-agents/) for how every AI command runs
through the local agent runtime.

## Pick a different model

`⌘K → "AI: Local Models (WebGPU)"` lists the curated catalog for this GPU
(size, tier, downloaded, recommended). "Automatic" lets the model manager
choose per task: small models for tags and completions, larger ones for
translation and documents, Hermes (function calling) when an agent needs
tools, Qwen2.5 Coder for the product builder.

## Privacy claim

When `useLocalAi` is on AND `localLlmAvailable().available === true`,
prompts never leave your tab. The only network requests web-llm makes
are the initial weight downloads (from `huggingface.co` mirrors) plus
optional telemetry that you can disable. No prompt content is
transmitted.
