pages.title: MCP and the lumen CLI
pages.description: Let Claude Desktop, Claude Code or your IDE search and read your vault — off by default, with scopes per client, and every change waits for your approval.
pages.md:
Lumen's vault can be used from outside the app in two ways:

- the **MCP server** (`@lumen-md/mcp-server`) for AI clients that speak the
  [Model Context Protocol](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/) — Claude
  Desktop, Claude Code, Cursor, VS Code, Zed;
- the **`lumen` CLI** for you at a terminal: `lumen search`, `open`, `new`,
  `append`, `daily`.

Both work on the vault folder on disk. Three rules hold everywhere:

1. **Off by default.** A client gets no tools until you enable it.
2. **Scopes per client.** You choose what each client may do.
3. **No write without approval.** A client's write is only a proposal; the
   note changes when you approve it.

## Install

The server is not published to npm yet, so build it from the repository (Node 22+):

```bash
git clone https://github.com/talstilkol/lumen-md
cd lumen-md/mcp-server
npm ci
npm run build          # → mcp-server/dist/index.js and dist/lumen.js
```

Until it is on npm, run `node /path/to/lumen-md/mcp-server/dist/lumen.js`
where this page says `npx -p @lumen-md/mcp-server lumen`, and use
`"command": "node", "args": ["/path/to/lumen-md/mcp-server/dist/index.js", "--client", "…"]`
where a client config says `npx -y @lumen-md/mcp-server`.

## Turn a client on

```bash
cd ~/Documents/Lumen            # your vault folder
npx -p @lumen-md/mcp-server lumen mcp enable claude-desktop --scopes search,read
npx -p @lumen-md/mcp-server lumen mcp status
```

| Scope | Tools |
|---|---|
| `search` | `search_notes` — BM25 over Hebrew and English (prefix letters ו ה ב ל מ ש כ and niqqud are handled) |
| `read` | `read_note`, `list_notes`, `list_tags`, `get_backlinks` |
| `propose` | `create_note`, `append_note`, `write_note`, `update_frontmatter` — proposals only |

`lumen mcp enable <client>` without `--scopes` grants `search,read`. Add
`propose` only for a client you want suggestions from. `lumen mcp disable
<client>` takes effect on its next call. The settings live in
`<vault>/.lumen/mcp.json`; clients cannot read or write anything under
`.lumen/` (or any other dot folder), `..` or absolute paths.

## Connect it

Give each client its own `--client` name — the one you enabled. (Without
it, the server uses the name the client reports when it connects.)

**Claude Desktop** — `~/Library/Application Support/Claude/claude_desktop_config.json`
(macOS; `%APPDATA%\Claude\` on Windows):

```json
{
  "mcpServers": {
    "lumen": {
      "command": "npx",
      "args": ["-y", "@lumen-md/mcp-server", "--client", "claude-desktop"],
      "env": { "LUMEN_VAULT": "/Users/you/Documents/Lumen" }
    }
  }
}
```

**Claude Code** — from any folder:

```bash
claude mcp add lumen -e LUMEN_VAULT="$HOME/Documents/Lumen" -- npx -y @lumen-md/mcp-server --client claude-code
npx -p @lumen-md/mcp-server lumen mcp enable claude-code --vault "$HOME/Documents/Lumen" --scopes search,read
```

**Cursor** (`~/.cursor/mcp.json`), **VS Code** (`.vscode/mcp.json`, key
`servers`) and **Zed** (`context_servers`) take the same command and
arguments: `npx -y @lumen-md/mcp-server --client cursor` (or `vscode`,
`zed`) with `LUMEN_VAULT` in `env`.

## Approving changes

A client's `create_note` / `append_note` / `write_note` /
`update_frontmatter` writes a proposal to `.lumen/mcp/pending/` and tells
the client nothing is written yet. You decide:

- **In Lumen:** the proposals appear in the review screen
  (⌘K → *AI: Review changes proposed by agents*, or the **Review** badge in
  the status bar) as "Proposed by claude-desktop (MCP client)", each as a
  diff. Approve writes the note; Reject drops it. This needs the vault
  folder in the app — the same folder, or synced with Git (`.lumen/` is
  synced like the notes).
- **In a terminal:**

  ```bash
  lumen mcp review              # every proposal as a diff
  lumen mcp approve <id>        # or --all
  lumen mcp reject <id>         # or --all
  ```

A proposal keeps the text it was computed from. If the note changed since,
approving writes nothing and the proposal is dropped as a conflict.

## The ledger

Every call — allowed, refused, proposed, approved, rejected — is a line in
`.lumen/mcp/ledger.jsonl`: time, client, tool, scope, note path, decision,
and how many bytes of your vault went to the client. Never the note text
or the query. `lumen mcp log` prints it.

## The `lumen` CLI

```bash
lumen search budget meeting      # path, title, matching line (exit 3: nothing found)
lumen open "Launch plan"         # opens it in your default app; --print to print it
lumen new ideas/one "first line" # creates; refuses if it exists
lumen append ideas/one.md "more"
lumen daily "call Dana"          # journal/YYYY-MM-DD.md, adds "- 09:05 call Dana"
```

The vault is `--vault <dir>`, else `$LUMEN_VAULT`, else the current folder.
`new`, `append` and `daily` are you at the keyboard, so they write directly
(logged as client `cli`). Install with `npm i -g @lumen-md/mcp-server`, or
run from a clone with `npm run lumen -- search …`.

## Speed

Search keeps an index in memory, built on the first search and brought up
to date before each one (only changed notes are read again). On 10,000
notes a search answers in well under 300 ms.

pages.description: Record a meeting, transcribe it on this device, and get its decisions, tasks with owner and date, and open questions — tasks in the task panel, dates in a calendar file.
pages.md:
`⌘K → "🎙 Meeting notes (record on this device)"` records a meeting; when
you stop, Whisper transcribes it **on this device** (as the voice memo
does) and the `meeting-writer` agent turns the transcript into notes. For a
transcript you already have, use `⌘K → "AI: Meeting Notes from a
Transcript"` on the note (or a selection).

## What you get

```markdown
## Meeting · 2026-11-09 · 🛡 local

### Decisions
- Ship on Tuesday

### Tasks
- [ ] Send the budget (@Avi) 📅 2026-11-18
- [ ] Find out who pays for the venue

### Open questions
- Who pays for the venue?
```

- **Tasks** are checkbox lines in the [tasks format](/workspace/tasks/)
  (`📅` for the due date), so they appear in the task panel's *Today* /
  *Upcoming* and in `tasks` blocks once the note is saved. The owner is kept
  in the text as `@name`.
- **Dates** the meeting mentions ("next Wednesday") are worked out from the
  meeting's day; a date that isn't a real `YYYY-MM-DD` date is sent back to
  the model once, and an owner or date nobody said is never added.
- **Calendar.** When tasks have dates, Lumen offers to save them as an
  `.ics` file (one to-do per task, due on its date) for any calendar app.
- The transcript stays below the notes, folded.

The agent runs through the agent runtime: under the *local only* policy on
a local model (Ollama or the in-browser model).

## Measuring it

`npm run eval:meetings` reads the owner's golden meetings (plan 7.10
`meetings`, 15.11 — never committed) from `LUMEN_EVAL_MEETINGS_DIR` and
reports the share of each meeting's reference action items the notes found
(target: ≥ 90 %).

pages.title: Meeting transcripts with speakers
pages.description: Transcribe a meeting recording on this device with who said what, name each speaker once, and get the meeting notes on top.
pages.md:
`⌘K → "🎙 Transcribe a meeting recording (who said what)…"` takes an audio
or video file of a meeting and inserts, at the cursor:

1. the [meeting notes](/ai/meeting-notes/) (decisions, tasks, open questions),
2. the transcript, one sentence per line, each with its speaker and a time
   that plays the recording from there,
3. a small `lumen-speaker-turns` block: who spoke when, used for renaming
   and for measuring accuracy.

```markdown
**Dana:** [▶ 0:07](<attachments/2026-11-10-weekly.m4a#t=7,10>) Hi everyone.
**Avi:** [▶ 0:10](<attachments/2026-11-10-weekly.m4a#t=10,14>) Let's start with the quarter's budget.
```

## How it works

Everything runs **on this device**:

- **Words**: the same Hebrew Whisper as
  [file transcription](/ai/whisper-desktop/) (ivrit.ai's model in
  whisper.cpp on the desktop app, or Whisper in the browser).
- **Speakers**: the two networks of pyannote speaker-diarization 3.1, run
  with ONNX Runtime. The segmentation network finds who is speaking in each
  10-second window (up to three people at once, overlaps included). A voice
  embedding is taken for each person in each window, and the embeddings are
  clustered into the meeting's speakers (S1, S2, …). Each sentence then
  gets the speaker who talks most during it.
- **Names**: for each speaker you're asked once for a name, with their
  longest sentence as a reminder. Leave it empty to keep `S1`.

The diarization models are downloaded only after you agree (the size is
shown first), from a pinned revision with its size and checksum checked,
and they're kept on the device. Until the owner has pinned them, the
transcript is inserted without speakers and a notice says so.

## Rename a speaker later

`⌘K → "Rename a speaker in this note…"` picks a speaker and renames them
everywhere in the note at once: every `**Name:**` label and the turns
block. Other text (for example a task that mentions `S1`) is left alone.

## Accuracy

The target is a diarization error rate (DER) of at most 20% on five Hebrew
golden recordings, and an hour of meeting processed in under 15 minutes on
a Mac M1. The DER is scored with
`node scripts/meetings/der.mjs --golden <dir>` against hand-checked RTTM
files; only numbers are printed.

sections.text: ⌘K → "🎙 Transcribe a meeting recording (who said what)…" takes an audio or video file of a meeting and inserts, at the cursor: 1. the meeting notes (decisions, tasks, open questions), 2. the transcript, one sentence per line, each with its speaker and a time that plays the recording from there, 3. a small lumen-speaker-turns block: who spoke when, used for renaming and for measuring accuracy.

sections.heading: How it works
sections.text: Everything runs on this device : Words : the same Hebrew Whisper as file transcription (ivrit.ai's model in whisper.cpp on the desktop app, or Whisper in the browser). Speakers : the two networks of pyannote speaker-diarization 3.1, run with ONNX Runtime. The segmentation network finds who is speaking in each 10-second window (up to three people at once, overlaps included). A voice embedding is taken for each person in each window, and the embeddings are clustered into the meeting's speakers (S1, S2, …). Each sentence then gets the speaker who talks most during it. Names : for each speaker you're asked once for a name, with their longest sentence as a reminder. Leave it empty to keep S1. The diarization models are downloaded only after you agree (the size is shown first), from a pinned revision with its size and checksum checked, and they're kept on the device. Until the owner has pinned them, the transcript is inserted without speakers and a notice says so.

sections.heading: Rename a speaker later
sections.text: ⌘K → "Rename a speaker in this note…" picks a speaker and renames them everywhere in the note at once: every Name: label and the turns block. Other text (for example a task that mentions S1) is left alone.

sections.heading: Accuracy
sections.text: The target is a diarization error rate (DER) of at most 20% on five Hebrew golden recordings, and an hour of meeting processed in under 15 minutes on a Mac M1. The DER is scored with node scripts/meetings/der.mjs --golden against hand-checked RTTM files; only numbers are printed.

pages.title: Measuring the local models
pages.description: npm run bench:models runs every local engine on its golden set in a real browser, with WebGPU, and writes time, memory and quality into models/registry.json.
pages.md:
Lumen's local engines are measured where they run: in a browser, through
the app's own code (the transformers.js worker, tesseract.js), on the
golden sets in `eval/golden/`. The numbers go into `models/registry.json`,
next to each model's licence.

## Run it

On a computer with a GPU:

```bash
npm ci
npx playwright install chromium     # once
npm run bench:models
```

The command:

1. Starts the Vite dev server and opens `bench/models.html` in Chromium,
   in a window, with WebGPU on.
2. For each engine:
   - Loads its model once, so it is downloaded and cached.
   - Opens a fresh page and measures that page.
3. Prints a table and writes the numbers to
   `eval/results/bench-models-<date>.json`.

Nothing in the table or the file is an item, an input or an output: only
numbers.

To store the numbers in the registry:

```bash
npm run bench:models -- --write
```

## What is measured

| Number | What it is |
|---|---|
| `loadMs` | Loading the model from the browser's cache (the first, downloading load is not counted unless `--no-prime`) |
| `prepareMs` | Work done once per part, such as embedding the corpus |
| `p50Ms`, `p95Ms` | Time per item |
| `rssPeakMB`, `rssDeltaMB` | Resident memory of the whole browser (page, workers, GPU process) at its peak, and above the idle page |
| `jsHeapPeakMB` | The page's JavaScript heap at its peak |
| `quality` | The set's own metric: nDCG@10 for retrieval, CER for OCR (per condition), WER and CER for speech |

GPU memory itself is not visible to a web page. The GPU process's
resident size, counted in `rssPeakMB`, is the closest number.

## Engines

| Engine | Set | Model |
|---|---|---|
| `bm25` | retrieval | none: the baseline, reported but never written |
| `bge-rerank` | retrieval | `onnx-community/bge-reranker-v2-m3-ONNX` over BM25's 20 candidates |
| `e5` | retrieval | `Xenova/multilingual-e5-small`, dense, over the whole corpus |
| `tesseract` | ocr-he | `tessdata_fast` heb + eng |
| `whisper-tiny`, `whisper-small`, `whisper-turbo` | asr-he | `onnx-community/whisper-*` |

An engine is a file in `src/bench/engines/`. It exports a `BenchEngine`
with an id, the golden set it is measured on, the registry ids of its
models, and three functions: `load`, an optional `prepare`, and `run`.
How a set is scored is in `scripts/bench/tasks.mjs`. A feature that adds
a local engine adds its adapter there, so the next run measures it.

## When numbers are not written

`--write` stores a result as `measured.<device>` of each of the engine's
models only when the result is real and complete:

- The run had no error.
- Every item of every part was measured: not with `--limit`, and on the
  test split no part is below its size.
- The engine is a model, not the baseline.
- A WebGPU run really ran on WebGPU, on a real GPU. A run that fell back
  to WebAssembly is not a WebGPU number. Neither is one on SwiftShader,
  the CPU emulation headless Chromium offers when there is no GPU.

## Options

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--engines a,b` | Only these engines |
| `--backends webgpu,wasm` | Also measure WebAssembly: the page is shown no WebGPU, so the app picks wasm as on such a device |
| `--split test --dir <dir>` | The held-out test split (built in CI) |
| `--limit N` | The first N items per part: a quick check, never written |
| `--channel chrome` | Installed Chrome instead of Playwright's Chromium |
| `--headless` | No window (WebGPU is less reliable this way) |
| `--url <url>` | Use a dev server that is already running |

pages.title: Real models day
pages.description: One command that runs every real-model eval on a machine with Ollama and a GPU, resumes after a stop, and writes one sealed report.
pages.md:
Most of Lumen's AI checks run against a **fake Ollama** in tests: they prove
the wiring (prompts, parsers, tool calls), not the quality of a model. The
real numbers need a real model on a real GPU. `npm run models:day` runs all
of them in one go.

## Before you start

```sh
npm ci
npm run models:day -- check
```

`check` runs nothing. It lists what is missing, with the exact install
command for each item:

- Node ≥ 22.6 and `npm ci`
- Ollama ≥ 0.5 (structured outputs), running (`ollama serve`)
- a GPU: 12 GB of VRAM, or Apple Silicon with at least 16 GB
- the models, by exact tag: `ollama pull gemma3:12b`, `ollama pull qwen2.5:7b`,
  `ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:1.5b`, `ollama pull qwen3:0.6b`,
  `ollama pull nomic-embed-text` (about 15 GB together)
- for dictation WER: Python 3 with `pip install -r scripts/golden/requirements.txt`, and ffmpeg
- for the browser engines: `npx playwright install chromium`

Missing models are pulled by the run itself unless you pass `--no-pull`.

## Run it

```sh
npm run models:day
```

`npm run models:day -- plan` shows the steps, what each one measures, and its
declared time. The default steps are declared at 3 hours or less on a 12 GB
GPU. A step whose script is not on the checked-out branch is **unavailable**
and names the PR that adds it. A step that needs something only you have,
like the meeting recordings (`--meetings-dir`), is **blocked**. Neither one
counts as a failure.

| Step | Measures |
|---|---|
| `agents-gemma3`, `agents-qwen` | every agent's cases (target ≥ 90 % and ≥ 80 %) |
| `pdf-chat` | answers cited to the right page, and citation nDCG@5 |
| `summarize` | summary sentences grounded in the source |
| `fim` | autocomplete latency p50 / p95 (target p50 < 300 ms) |
| `real-tiny` | every agent once on `qwen3:0.6b` |
| `rerank` | the reranker on HeQ |
| `asr-zipformer`, `asr-web` | dictation WER on FLEURS-he validation (target ≤ 15 %) |
| `tool-calls` | valid tool calls on both models (target ≥ 95 %) |
| `bench-models` | every browser engine in Chromium on WebGPU |
| `meetings`, `canvas-draw`, `crosslingual`, `lit-review` | each feature's own eval |
| `dictalm3` (optional: `--with dictalm3`) | DictaLM 3.0 against `qwen3:4b` |

## Stop and continue

Each step's result is saved as soon as the step ends. Press Ctrl-C at any
point and run the same command again: finished steps are kept, and the step
that was running starts over. Use `--redo <step>` to run a finished step
again, or `--fresh` to start a new run.

## The report

Everything goes to `eval/results/day/<run>/`:

- `<step>/`: the eval's own files, plus `log.txt`
- `report.md`: a table per step and per agent, and which plan task each step covers
- `report.json`: the commit, the machine, the GPU, each model's Ollama
  digest, and every file with its sha256. A **receipt** (a sha256 over the
  whole report) seals it.

Pass `--sign-key key.pem` to also sign the receipt with Ed25519 (make a key
with `openssl genpkey -algorithm ed25519 -out key.pem`). To check a report:

```sh
npm run models:day -- verify eval/results/day/<run>/report.json
```

This fails if the report or any result file changed after the run. If the
server was the fake one from the tests (`npm run fake-ollama`), the whole
report says **WIRING RUN, NOT A MODEL SCORE**.

pages.title: Hebrew niqqud on this device
pages.description: Add or remove vowel points (niqqud) in Hebrew text with a model that runs in your browser.
pages.md:
Three commands in `⌘K`, on the selection — or the whole note when nothing
is selected:

| Command | What it does |
|---|---|
| **Hebrew: add niqqud** | Points every Hebrew word. Existing points are replaced. |
| **Hebrew: add partial niqqud** | Points only the words the model finds ambiguous, the way modern texts point a word that could be read two ways. |
| **Hebrew: remove niqqud** | Strips the points. Needs no model. |

English, code, numbers and punctuation pass through unchanged. Before
anything is written, Lumen checks that the letters themselves did not
change — only points are added or removed.

## The model

[Nakdimon](https://github.com/elazarg/nakdimon) (Elazar Gershuni, MIT,
≈ 21 MB) runs in a background worker with ONNX Runtime on WebAssembly,
so it works on any device, without a GPU and offline once downloaded.
It is downloaded only after a dialog that shows its size, licence and
attribution, verified against the checksum in `models/registry.json`,
and kept on this device.

The download is served from Lumen's own model host, which is not set up
yet; until then *add niqqud* says the model is not available, and
*remove niqqud* works as usual.

## Measured

On the dev split of the `nikud` golden set, with
`node scripts/golden/evals/nikud.mjs --dev --model Nakdimon.onnx`:

| Part | Sentences | Words fully right | Letters with a wrong mark |
|---|---|---|---|
| Modern (Nakdimon's own held-out test texts) | 10 | 93.6% | 2.8% |
| Classical (Ben-Yehuda: poetry, liturgy) | 15 | 54.9% | 21.3% |
| Letters unchanged (all) | 25 | 100% | — |

Nakdimon is trained on modern Hebrew; classical and poetic text needs the
larger "high quality" model below.

## High quality: DictaBERT-char-menaked

[DictaBERT-char-menaked](https://huggingface.co/dicta-il/dictabert-large-char-menaked)
(DICTA, CC BY 4.0) is the model behind Dicta's Nakdan, the reference for
Hebrew niqqud. Lumen runs it as an int8 ONNX model in the same background
worker. When it is published on Lumen's model host, *add niqqud* offers it
first, with its own dialog (size, licence, attribution). Decline once and
this device keeps using Nakdimon. Either way, every result passes the same
letters-unchanged check before anything is written.

Until the model is exported and published, Nakdimon is used; nothing
changes in how the commands behave.

## Other readings of a word

After *add niqqud*, every pointed word remembers its next most likely
readings, as in Dicta's Nakdan:

- words the model found ambiguous get a **dotted underline** — click one to
  see its readings, with how likely each is;
- **Alt+click** any pointed word to see its readings too;
- pick a reading to replace the word; **Esc** closes the list.

The readings come from the model's own probabilities for each letter, so
they cost no second model run. Every reading keeps the word's letters.

*Add partial niqqud* points only the ambiguous words, and the same list is
there for them. Pointing only nouns or only verbs needs a part-of-speech
tagger, which Lumen does not have yet.

pages.title: On-device OCR (Hebrew, English, columns)
pages.description: How Lumen reads text from images and scanned PDF pages on your device — Latin words inside Hebrew lines, multi-column pages, and the reading order of the result.
pages.md:
When you import a scanned PDF, or an image that is mostly text, Lumen reads
it **on this device** with Tesseract (LSTM, `tessdata_fast` Hebrew and
English models that ship with the app). No image leaves the device and OCR
makes no outside request.

## Latin words inside Hebrew lines

Hebrew text is full of foreign terms: `ב-Zoom`, `קובץ ה-PDF`,
`info@example.org`, `ו-Bluetooth`. A plain Hebrew+English OCR pass gets
these wrong in typical ways:

- the Hebrew prefix glued to a Latin word is read as a Latin symbol
  (`ו-Bluetooth` → `Bluetooth-1`), and the line comes out in visual order;
- the Latin word after a prefix is read as Hebrew shapes
  (`ו-Bluetooth` → `ו-ח01סז6טו8`);
- a short Hebrew word between Latin words is read as Latin (`או` → `IN`).

Lumen fixes only the lines that need it, from the recogniser's own word and
letter boxes: the doubtful word is read again with a Hebrew-only or
Latin-only pass, a reading is kept only when it is a real word (a Hebrew
reading with digits among the letters, or a final letter inside the word,
is not), and the line is rebuilt in **logical order** — right to left, each
left-to-right run (`Google Drive`) read left to right, the prefix before
the whole run (`ב-Google Drive`).

## Columns and reading order

On a page with two or three columns the recogniser may list the left
column first, run a line across the gap between columns, or put a heading
that spans the page between them. Lumen orders the lines from their boxes:

1. a line that crosses a column gap is cut there;
2. the page is split into bands (a heading, the columns, a footer), top to
   bottom;
3. inside a band, columns are read **right to left** on a Hebrew page (left
   to right on an English one), each top to bottom.

The text you get — in a note, or copied from a scanned page — follows that
order.

## Text layer of a scanned page

Each recognised line keeps its box, so a scanned page can carry an
invisible, selectable text layer over the image: one span per line, in
reading order, holding the line's logical text with its direction. Selecting
and copying Hebrew from the page then gives the words in the order they are
read, not the order of the glyphs on screen.

## How it is measured

The Hebrew OCR golden set (`eval/golden/ocr-he`) has rendered lines and
pages in six fonts, clean and degraded, and a part of 20 mixed-script pages in
two or three columns. The CI measurement (`OCR_CER=1`,
`e2e/ocr-cer.spec.ts`) gates the character error rate per script (clean
≤ 5 %, degraded ≤ 12 %) and, on the column pages, the share of lines whose
words come out in reading order (≥ 95 %).

## Limits

- Handwriting and very low-resolution photos are out of scope.
- Narrow columns in a serif face are the hardest case: the recogniser can
  drop words there, and no reordering brings them back.
- Nikud is not read reliably; pointed lines are reported, not gated.

Lumen orders the lines from their boxes: 1. a line that crosses a column gap is cut there; 2. the page is split into bands (a heading, the columns, a footer), top to bottom; 3. inside a band, columns are read right to left on a Hebrew page (left to right on an English one), each top to bottom. The text you get — in a note, or copied from a scanned page — follows that order.

sections.heading: Text layer of a scanned page
sections.text: Each recognised line keeps its box, so a scanned page can carry an invisible, selectable text layer over the image: one span per line, in reading order, holding the line's logical text with its direction. Selecting and copying Hebrew from the page then gives the words in the order they are read, not the order of the glyphs on screen.

sections.heading: How it is measured
sections.text: The Hebrew OCR golden set (eval/golden/ocr-he) has rendered lines and pages in six fonts, clean and degraded, and a part of 20 mixed-script pages in two or three columns. The CI measurement (OCR CER=1, e2e/ocr-cer.spec.ts) gates the character error rate per script (clean ≤ 5 %, degraded ≤ 12 %) and, on the column pages, the share of lines whose words come out in reading order (≥ 95 %).

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text: Handwriting and very low-resolution photos are out of scope. Narrow columns in a serif face are the hardest case: the recogniser can drop words there, and no reordering brings them back. Nikud is not read reliably; pointed lines are reported, not gated.

pages.title: Organize the vault
pages.description: Missing links, tags, duplicates to merge and maps of content for your whole vault — each one a change you approve, with its confidence, reason and a quote.
pages.md:
**⌘K → AI: Organize the vault** reads every note and suggests:

| Suggestion | What changes when you approve it |
|---|---|
| **Link** — a note mentions another note's title but does not link to it | The first mention becomes `[[Title]]` (or `[[Title|the words used]]`). A Hebrew prefix letter stays outside the link: `ב[[פרויקט אלפא]]`. Mentions in code, headings, URLs and existing links are left alone. |
| **Tags** — a tag the vault already uses fits a note that lacks it | Up to three tags are added to the note's front matter. Reason: the tag's word is in the note, or the notes it links with have the tag. |
| **Merge** — two notes are near duplicates | The longer note gets the other's extra paragraphs under its title; the other becomes a pointer `→ [[kept note]]`. |
| **Map of content** — a tag has six or more notes and no note links most of them | A new note `maps/<tag>.md` that lists them. |

## Nothing is written without you

The organizer only suggests. The panel shows each suggestion with its
**confidence**, **why**, and a **quote** from the note it is based on.
**Review the next 20** sends a batch to the review screen (the same one
agents use), where each suggestion is a diff with Approve and Reject.
Only Approve writes, and only if the text is still what the organizer
read. Link and tag changes in one note can be approved in any order.

While it reads the vault you can **Pause**, **Resume** or **Cancel**, as
with batch jobs. Cancelling writes nothing.

## It learns what you accept

Every approval and rejection is remembered on this device (IndexedDB,
like the agents' learning critic): kinds of suggestion you approve rise,
ones you reject sink, and a kind you rejected again and again (at least 3
times, under 25% approved) is no longer suggested. A tag you keep
rejecting stops being suggested on its own.

## How it decides

The analysis runs on this device without a model: whole-word title
matches (with Hebrew prefix letters and niqqud handled), the tags of
linked notes, word 5-gram overlap for duplicates. One-word titles that
are ordinary words in your vault ("Notes", "סיכום") are not linked. A
local model can be plugged in to re-score suggestions (`setOrganizerModel`);
none is on by default.

pages.title: Personal data before the cloud
pages.description: When your AI policy lets a request leave this device, Lumen hides e-mails, phone numbers, ID numbers, cards, IBANs, plates and birth dates on the device first, and puts them back in the answer.
pages.md:
Under the **local only** policy nothing leaves your device, so there is
nothing to hide. Under **local first** or **cloud**, a request can go to
a cloud provider (OpenAI, Anthropic, Gemini or Mistral). Before it does,
Lumen redacts personal data **on this device**:

| What | How it is recognised |
|---|---|
| E-mail address | the address pattern |
| Phone number | Israeli mobile and landline formats, `+972`, international with separators |
| ID number (ת״ז) | 9 digits **with a valid check digit** |
| Payment card | 13–19 digits that pass the **Luhn** check |
| IBAN | the IBAN format **with a valid mod-97 check** |
| Licence plate | Israeli formats `12-345-67` and `123-45-678` |
| Birth date | a date next to a birth word ("תאריך לידה", "נולד", "born", "DOB") |
| Names | with the Hebrew name model (DictaBERT-NER, CC BY 4.0) downloaded |

Each value becomes a token such as `⟨EMAIL_1⟩`. The same value always
gets the same token within one request, so the model can still refer to
it. When the answer comes back, the tokens are replaced with the
originals, including in streamed answers.

Numbers that only look like personal data are left alone. This covers an
order number, a parcel code, a product code, an ID with a wrong check
digit, a card number that fails Luhn, and historical or event dates.

## Settings

**AI settings → Personal data before the cloud** (shown when the policy
is not *local only*):

- **Hide personal data before a request leaves this device.** This is on
  by default.
- **Show what will be sent before each cloud request.** Before each cloud
  request you see the redacted text and a count per type, and can cancel.

The **privacy ledger** (`⌘K → Privacy ledger…`) shows how many items
were hidden in how many requests. It shows the counts only, never the
values.

## Names

Names have no pattern. Hebrew names are found by DictaBERT-NER, a model
that runs on your device. A cloud request never downloads it; you
download it with consent, after seeing its size and licence, under
**Settings → Models**. Without it, only the patterns above are hidden,
and names are sent as written.

## How it is measured

- **Patterns:** on the dev split of the PII golden set
  (`eval/golden/ner-pii`), recall is 100% and precision is 100%, with 0
  false redactions on the 13 hard negatives. On 3000 generated items
  (1000 hard negatives) there were 0 false redactions. The test is
  `src/__tests__/piiGolden.test.ts`.
- **In the browser:** an end-to-end test puts every pattern item of the
  set in a note and sends it to a stubbed cloud provider. None of the
  values reaches the provider (`e2e/pii-redaction.spec.ts`).
- **The held-out test split** is scored in CI by
  `scripts/golden/evals/ner-pii.mjs`.

pages.title: Privacy and the AI policy
pages.description: What stays on your device, the one setting that decides whether AI may ever use the cloud, and the ledger that records every AI network request.
pages.md:
By default nothing you write leaves this device. Notes are kept in the
browser's private storage, or in a folder on the desktop. They go
somewhere else only when **you** turn on sync, collaboration, or a cloud
AI provider.

## The AI policy

`⌘K → AI: Local or Cloud Policy` decides where an AI request may go:

| Policy | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Local only** | nothing leaves this device: Ollama, the in-browser WebGPU model and transformers.js only. A cloud provider is **never** contacted, not even as a fallback when no local model can answer. |
| **Local first** | local models first; a cloud provider (with your own key) only when none of them can answer |
| **Cloud** | the cloud provider you selected is used directly |

A **fresh install starts on *Local only***. An installation that was set
up for the cloud before policies existed keeps its behaviour (*Cloud*
when a cloud provider was selected, *Local first* when only a key was
configured), so an upgrade never silently changes where your prompts go.

## The privacy ledger

`⌘K → Privacy ledger…` lists every network request the AI features made:
the time, the host, how many bytes went out and came back, why
(cloud AI, a model download, research…), the policy at that moment, and
whether it was **allowed or blocked**. A request the policy forbids is
blocked before it leaves the machine and still appears in the ledger, so
you can see that it was stopped.

The ledger stores **no** prompt, response or header, only the facts above.
It covers AI traffic: provider calls, embeddings, transcription, grammar,
research and model downloads, including the OCR language models fetched
from a worker. Fonts, sync and the app's own files are not AI traffic and
aren't listed.

## Everything else

| Data | Where it lives | Leaves the device? |
|---|---|---|
| Your notes | the browser's private file system (OPFS), or a folder on the desktop | only with sync or collaboration on |
| Settings, search history | this browser's storage | no |
| API keys and tokens | encrypted on this device; the OS keychain in the desktop app ([details](/security/vault/)) | only to the service each one belongs to |
| Collaboration | peer to peer (WebRTC); end-to-end encrypted when the room has a password ([details](/collab/encryption/)) | only to the people in the room |
| Error reports | off unless whoever hosts the app sets `VITE_SENTRY_DSN` at build time | only then |

The full policy is in `PRIVACY.md` in the repository.

pages.title: Read aloud (Hebrew included)
pages.description: Listen to a note on this device — the word being read is highlighted, the position is kept, and you choose the speed and voice.
pages.md:
**Command palette → Read aloud** reads the open note on this device. Run it
again to stop. This works for articles you clipped, too: open the note and
listen.

- **What is being read is highlighted**: the sentence, and the word when the
  voice reports where each word starts (most system voices do). The
  highlight is a mark, not a selection, so you can keep typing.
- **It continues where you stopped.** Stop in the middle, run it again later,
  and it resumes at the same sentence, even if you edited the note. After the
  last sentence the next run starts from the top.
- **Speed and voice**: *Command palette → Read aloud: voice and speed…*. Pick
  the speed (0.75× – 2×) and, when your system has more than one voice for
  the note's language, which one to use. A ☁ next to a voice means the
  system streams it from the internet; the others run on the device.
- Code blocks, front matter and link addresses are skipped. Each sentence is
  read in its own language: a Hebrew sentence with the Hebrew voice, an
  English one with the English voice.

## Hebrew voices

Hebrew is read with **your system's Hebrew voice** (on macOS, Windows and
Android). If there is none, Lumen says so; add one in the system's speech
settings.

Lumen also has an on-device **neural** Hebrew reader. It adds niqqud
([Hebrew niqqud on this device](/ai/nikud/)), turns the pointed text into
phonemes with Lumen's own Hebrew rules, and plays them with a Piper-format
voice. It is **not active yet**: every public Hebrew voice is trained on
recordings that may not be used commercially, so none can ship. Once a voice
with a licence that allows it exists, it is listed in the licence gate,
downloads once with your consent, and Hebrew notes are read with it. After
that download, reading needs no network.

## Listening test (developers)

The read-aloud quality target is an average score (MOS) of at least 3.8 out
of 5, from 5 listeners on 20 everyday sentences (`eval/listening/tts-he.json`).

```sh
npm run tts:mos -- sheet --raters dana,yossi,noa,eli,maya   # score sheet + a note to read aloud
npm run tts:mos -- score tts-ratings.csv                       # MOS, 95% interval, per sentence and listener
```

pages.title: Search reranking — measured
pages.description: What the search reranker adds on Lumen's retrieval golden set, the decision that follows, and how to measure the model yourself.
pages.md:
Search ranks with BM25 (and, in smart search, embeddings). A **reranker**
then reorders the best candidates by reading the query and each candidate
together. Lumen has two:

| Reranker | Where | Default |
|---|---|---|
| built-in (lexical) | every device; Hebrew-aware word coverage blended with the retrieval rank; no download | on |
| model: `bge-reranker-v2-m3` (Apache-2.0) | WebGPU browsers and the desktop app only; a one-time download of about 571 MB (q8), after you agree | **off** |

`jina-reranker-v2` is not used (its licence is non-commercial), and
mMiniLM rerankers don't cover Hebrew.

## The measurement

On the retrieval golden set (plan 7.1, `eval/golden/retrieval`), HeQ dev
split — 12 Hebrew questions over 238 paragraphs, 20 BM25 candidates each,
nDCG@10:

| | nDCG@10 |
|---|---|
| BM25 alone | 1.0000 |
| BM25 + built-in reranker | 1.0000 |

BM25 already puts every answer first on this split, so no reranker can add
the 5 points the plan asks for: **the model reranker stays off by default**
and is offered only where it runs fast, after consent. The cross-lingual
part (Belebele, an English question over Hebrew passages, where BM25 can't
match and a reranker might help) and the held-out test split are measured
with the model by:

```sh
npm run eval:rerank
# with the held-out split and Belebele built:
LUMEN_EVAL_RERANK_DIRS=eval/golden/retrieval/dev,<test split dir> npm run eval:rerank
```

It writes `eval/results/rerank-<date>.md` with BM25, BM25 + the model and the
gain per part, and the decision the plan's rule gives (< 5 points: off by
default).

pages.title: Research and citation checks
pages.description: Ask a question and get a note with a quoted source for every claim; check the citations in any note.
pages.md:
## Research: Ask a Question

Command: `🔎 Research: Ask a Question…`.

Lumen searches the web, reads the sources and writes a new note. The
note starts with a short summary, followed by sections, and every claim
carries a footnote. Each footnote holds the passage from the source
that supports the claim:

```md
Roses are pruned in early spring.[^1]

[^1]: [Rose guide](https://example.org/roses) — “Prune roses in early spring, when buds swell.”
```

Choose how Lumen searches with `🔎 Research: Settings…`:

| Search | Needs | How it works |
|---|---|---|
| **Claude web search** (default) | AI provider set to Claude (Anthropic) | One request: Claude searches (up to 5 searches), reads and answers. The quotes are copied word for word from the pages by Anthropic. Anthropic bills the searches separately from tokens. |
| **SearXNG** / **Brave Search** / **Tavily** | The research service on this deployment (a local SearXNG needs no key; Brave and Tavily need yours) | The **researcher agent** runs on your AI model, local first, in a tool loop. It searches (`search_web`), reads the pages it chooses (`fetch_page`), and copies the passages it cites (`extract_quotes`). Then Lumen **checks every quote against the page it came from**, outside the model. A quote that can't be found is marked ⚠️ in the note. If fewer than half of the quotes are in their pages, the agent tries once more and is told to quote word for word. |

Under the **local only** AI policy:
- **With a remote research service:** the same agent answers from your **clip library** (`Library/`, `ספרייה/`) and nothing leaves the device.
- **With a research service on this machine:** every search and every page read asks you first. Only the search query, or the page address, is sent.

Every page is outside content: the agent gets it cleaned and delimited, and instructions planted in it are flagged (see Local agents → Outside content). The note is saved with `untrusted: true` in its frontmatter.

Pages the research read but didn't cite are listed under "Also read".
Every model call appears in `AI: Usage & Cost This Month`. A research
run counts as one prompt against your plan's AI quota.

## Research: Verify Citations in This Note

Command: `🔎 Research: Verify Citations in This Note`.

This works on any note, not only research output. Lumen reads the
footnotes that link to web pages and checks each one:

| Result | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ✅ quote found | The quoted passage is on the page. Quote marks, dashes, case and spacing don't need to match exactly. |
| 🟡 found approximately | At least 85% of the quote's words appear close together on the page. A quote longer than 200 words is scored on samples, so it is "approximate" unless it is on the page word for word. |
| ❌ quote not found | The page is reachable, but the passage isn't on it. |
| 💀 dead link | The page returned an HTTP error. |
| ⚠️ couldn't read | The address was blocked, the page isn't HTML or text, or the request timed out. |
| 🔗 reachable | The footnote has no quote, so only the link was checked. |

Footnotes can be written as `[^1]: [Title](url) — “quote”`, as
`[^1]: url "quote"`, or as just a link.

## The research service

Reading pages and Brave / Tavily searches go through a small worker that
your deployment runs (`edge-workers/research`, set with
`VITE_RESEARCH_ENDPOINT`). Browsers can't fetch other sites directly.

- It only reads public http(s) pages, never internal addresses.
- It reads at most 2 MB per page.
- It forwards no cookies.
- Your search key is passed through for each request and is never
  stored.
- It only answers your app's own origins.
- It requires a shared token (`RESEARCH_TOKEN`). You enter it under AI
  settings → Research token; it is kept in the app's secret store and is
  never built into the app. A token entered there is sent only to the
  research address that was in use when you saved it. Without a token
  configured, the service refuses every request.

Claude web search doesn't need the service.

## Known limitations — status

| Id | Limitation | Status |
|---|---|---|
| A7 | Approximate quote matching is a heuristic with a compute budget | Decision: kept. The check runs on your device, so a long quote is scored on up to 5 samples of 200 words. A quote is ✅ only when it is on the page word for word; a full score on the samples alone is 🟡 "checked on samples". |
| A8 | No real authentication without accounts | Fixed in part. The token is now required: a service without one refuses everything. In a public web app the token ships in the app, so it only stops casual reuse. To restrict who may use it, put the service behind Cloudflare Access and add a rate-limiting rule. |

sections.text: Reading pages and Brave / Tavily searches go through a small worker that your deployment runs (edge-workers/research, set with VITE RESEARCH ENDPOINT). pages.description: Spell-check English notes with a dictionary that ships with Lumen — no LanguageTool account, no request leaves the device.
pages.md:
Lumen's grammar check (`⌘K → Check grammar (LanguageTool)`, and the background
underlines when *Grammar check* is on) has three backends. Which one runs
depends on the AI policy and on what you configured:

| | Under *local only* | Under *local first* / *cloud* |
|---|---|---|
| LanguageTool on this machine or network (`lumen.grammar.endpoint`, e.g. `docker/local-ai.yml` on port 8010) | used | used |
| The public LanguageTool API (`api.languagetool.org`) | **never contacted** | used |
| English dictionary on this device (this page) | used | — |
| Local proofreader model | added when you run the check yourself | — |

Hebrew paragraphs are always checked on this device (rules plus the
optional Hspell dictionary) and never sent anywhere.

## What it checks

- **Words**, against the en-US Hunspell dictionary
  ([dictionary-en](https://github.com/wooorm/dictionaries/tree/main/dictionaries/en)
  4.0, SCOWL word list, MIT AND BSD) through
  [nspell](https://github.com/wooorm/nspell) (MIT), in a background worker.
  The dictionary (≈ 0.55 MB) is part of the app: nothing is downloaded.
- **Only English paragraphs.** Each paragraph's language is detected on
  this device; a French or German paragraph is not marked as misspelled
  English. A paragraph too short to tell follows the rest of the note.
- **Only prose.** Code blocks, inline code, front matter, URLs, e-mail
  addresses, link targets, wiki links, footnote labels, `#tags`, HTML tags,
  ALL-CAPS acronyms, camelCase names and words with digits are skipped.

Hover an underline for up to three suggestions.

## Measured

On the committed dev split of the `spell-en` golden set (25 Moby-Dick
sentences with 32 injected typos), checked by
`node scripts/golden/evals/spell-en.mjs --dev` and by the unit tests:

| Metric | Result | Target |
|---|---|---|
| Typos found | 100% | ≥ 90% |
| First suggestion is the right word | 62.5% | — |
| Right word among the first five | 84.4% | — |
| Correct words marked wrong (clean sentences) | 2.6% | ≤ 3% |

Most false marks are names (*Queequeg*, *Stubb*) and British spellings
(*honour*): the dictionary is American English. The held-out test split
is scored by CI with the set's secret seed.

## Limits

- American English only; other Latin-script languages get no spelling
  check under *local only* unless you run LanguageTool yourself.
- Spelling, not grammar: "their is" passes. For grammar, run LanguageTool
  on this machine or use the explicit check, which adds the local
  proofreader model.
- There is no personal word list yet.

pages.title: Grounded summaries on this device
pages.description: Summaries made on this device whose every sentence is copied from the text and checked against it — Chrome's Summarizer for English, a local model for Hebrew, and a model-free fallback.
pages.md:
`⌘K → "AI: Summarize This Note (on this device)"` and **Summarize** in the
[Ask a PDF](/workspace/pdf-chat/) panel make a short summary in which
**every sentence is copied from the text** — shortened with "…" where words
were left out — and checked against it word for word (`quoteContained`, the
rule the research citations use). A sentence that isn't in the text is
never shown. In a PDF each sentence links to its page and line.

## Layers

| Layer | When | What |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome's Summarizer API | English text, and the browser already has its model | Chrome's on-device summary — used only if at least 95 % of its sentences are in the text (it often paraphrases) |
| Local model | otherwise | the `summarizer` agent on Ollama or the in-browser model — **local executors only**, under any AI policy. For Hebrew, DictaLM 3.0 1.7B in Ollama when it is installed; else the runtime's local pick (Qwen3 in web-llm in the browser). A long text is summarised section by section, then once more over the section summaries. |
| Extractive | no local model, or nothing usable | the sentences that carry the text's most frequent content words, in their order — no model at all |

Chrome's Summarizer doesn't support Hebrew, so a Hebrew text always goes to
the local model. A model whose answer has fewer than 80 % of its sentences
in the text is asked once more, with the reason.

Install the Hebrew model in Ollama (it is listed in its library as DictaLM
3.0), and Lumen picks it for Hebrew summaries by its name.

## Measuring it

`npm run eval:summarize` summarises the documents of the golden summary set
(plan 7.10, `eval/golden/summarize`) on your Ollama and reports the share of
the model's sentences that pass the grounding check **before** any is
dropped (target: ≥ 95 %), with key-word coverage as a second signal.
`LUMEN_EVAL_SUMMARY_DIRS` adds the held-out test split built with the golden
seed, for all 20 documents.

pages.title: Reliable tool calls on small local models
pages.description: How Lumen keeps a 7–12B local model's tool calls valid. Every call is held to a JSON schema, common slips are repaired, and an invalid call gets one retry before Lumen asks you.
pages.md:
Agents use tools to do their work: they search your notes, read a file,
or propose a change. A cloud model rarely gets a tool call wrong. A small
model on your own computer, like `qwen2.5:7b` or `gemma3:12b`, often does.
Lumen does four things about it.

## 1. Every call is held to a schema

On Ollama 0.5 or later, Lumen sends a JSON schema with every turn of a
local model (Ollama's *structured outputs*). The model can only answer with
a call to one of the agent's tools, with that tool's arguments, or with
the final answer. Cloud models above the small tier still use their own
native tool calls.

## 2. Common slips are repaired

Even with a schema, small models make the same slips again and again.
Lumen fixes these before it checks the call:

- the call in a different format (`{"name", "arguments"}`, `{"function": …}`,
  `{"action", "action_input"}`)
- the arguments sent as a JSON string, or wrapped in an extra object
- the tool name in another case (`SearchNotes` for `search_notes`)
- a key in another case (`Query` for `query`)
- a number or yes/no sent as text, or one value where a list is expected
- an extra property the tool doesn't take
- trailing commas, curly quotes, and Python's `True` / `None`

Lumen never invents a value you didn't give. If something required is
missing, the call stays invalid.

## 3. One retry, then a question for you

After an invalid call, the model sees what was wrong and the tool's exact
schema, and gets one more try. If that call is invalid too, the agent stops
and asks you to say what's needed. It doesn't guess.

## 4. Nothing is written without your approval

A repaired call goes through the same checks as any other call:
permissions, the network gate, and the approval screen for changes. A
repair can't make a call do more than it was allowed to do.

## How it's measured

There are 200 requests, 100 in Hebrew and 100 in English, over ten of the
agents' tools. Each request offers five tools, and only one is right.

```sh
npm run eval:tool-calls -- --models qwen2.5:7b,gemma3:12b
```

The target is at least 95% valid calls on both models. A valid call means
the right tool with arguments that match its schema. The report also shows
how many calls the old parser would have accepted, how many were repaired
or retried, and how many ended with a question to you. The same run is one
step of `npm run models:day`.

pages.title: Translation review (the UI's seven languages)
pages.description: The agent that checks every translation of Lumen's interface against its English — missing variables, odd lengths, untranslated strings and, on this machine, a back-translation.
pages.md:
Lumen's interface is translated into seven languages (Arabic, German,
French, Hebrew, Japanese, Russian, Chinese). `npm run i18n:review` checks
every translation against its English source and prints a report:

| Check | Level | What it means |
|---|---|---|
| missing variable | error | a `{placeholder}` of the English is not in the translation — the UI would lose the value |
| extra variable | error | a `{placeholder}` the English doesn't have — it would show literally |
| length | warning | far shorter or longer than the English (Japanese and Chinese have their own bounds) |
| untranslated | warning | the English word for word (product and format names are fine) |
| deviation | warning | with `--back`: translated back to English **on this machine** (M2M100 through transformers.js — no cloud), it shares little with the English (chrF < 25) |
| missing key | info | no translation yet; the UI shows English |

The command exits with status 1 when there is any error, and the test
`src/__tests__/i18nReview.test.ts` holds the seven locales at **0 missing
variables**.

```sh
node scripts/extract-i18n-keys.mjs          # refresh i18n/keys.json first
npm run i18n:review -- --out review.md      # the report
npm run i18n:review -- --back --sample 200  # with back-translation (downloads M2M100 once)
```

The first run fixed 34 missing variables — strings in six languages that had
been cut at an escaped quote (`git.alert.cloned`, `collab.prompt.join`,
`tree.confirm.deleteFile`, `tree.confirm.deleteFolder`) and a German and
French `writingGoal.done` without its numbers.

pages.title: Local translation
pages.description: Translate a document on this device, in three layers — Chrome's built-in translator, Opus-MT for Hebrew ⇄ English, M2M100 for the rest — with code and links kept exactly.
pages.md:
`⌘K → AI: Translate Document` translates the whole note into the language
you name. Since plan 6.4 the translation runs **on this device** whenever a
local layer can take the language pair; the cloud or local LLM is the last
resort, not the first.

## The three layers

| Layer | What | Languages | Download |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 · Chrome's built-in translator | Chrome's on-device Translator API | the language packs Chrome offers (Hebrew included) | a language pack, managed by Chrome, after your consent |
| 2 · Opus-MT | `opus-mt-en-he` (Apache-2.0) and `opus-mt-tc-big-he-en` (CC BY 4.0), converted to ONNX by Lumen, running in transformers.js in a worker | English ⇄ Hebrew | once, through the consent dialog below |
| 3 · M2M100 | `M2M100-418M` (MIT), same worker | about 100 languages, any pair | once, through the consent dialog |
| 3b · the AI model | the translator agent (your configured LLM) | any | — |

Which layer runs is decided by **measured quality**: each layer's chrF on the
`mt-he-en` golden set (NTREX-128, both directions) is recorded in
`src/ai/mt/quality.json`. Opus-MT is the baseline; a layer measured below
it for a pair is never chosen automatically. A layer whose quality has not
been measured yet may still run, and the toast says so ("its quality on
this pair is not measured yet").

The document's language is detected locally (plan 6.5), paragraph by
paragraph: a paragraph already in the target language is left as it is.

## Nothing downloads without asking

Before the first use of Opus-MT or M2M100 a dialog shows what the model
is for, its **size** (hundreds of MB), its **licence** and **attribution**,
and asks. A yes downloads the files once; Opus-MT's files are checked
against the checksums in `models/registry.json` and kept in this browser's
private storage (OPFS). A no leaves the document untouched and the
translation falls through to the next layer that is already available, or
to the AI model. Nothing you write is sent anywhere by the local layers.

Until the converted models are hosted (plan 15.9) layer 2 reports
"the converted models have no host yet", and the toast after a translation
lists the reason each local layer did not run.

## What never changes

Fenced and indented code, inline code, math, YAML frontmatter, every link
and image target, wiki links, autolinks, bare URLs, e-mail addresses,
footnote marks and HTML tags are kept exactly as they were. Only the words
move: headings, list items, quotes and table cells keep their markers. If a
model disturbs a protected span, the line is translated again run by run,
and the result is checked before it replaces your text.

## Measuring

```sh
node scripts/golden/evals/mt.mjs --dev --models <folder with the converted models>
```

prints chrF per layer and direction on the dev split of `mt-he-en`;
`--write-quality` records the numbers that decide the automatic choice. A
layer the harness cannot run where it is executed is reported as
"not measured", with the reason, never as a number.

pages.title: Voice commands, on this device
pages.description: Say "new note", "search…" or "add task…" in Hebrew or English. Lumen recognises the speech and the command locally, and asks before anything that deletes.
pages.md:
Run **Voice command** from the command palette, then say one command. Lumen
listens for one sentence (up to 8 seconds), recognises it with the
dictation model on your device, and runs the matching command. Nothing is
sent anywhere: the speech model is the one dictation already downloaded,
and the command is matched against a fixed list of phrases.

The first time, start dictation once to download the model (74 MB).

## What you can say

| Say (Hebrew / English) | What happens |
|---|---|
| ״צור פתק חדש בשם…״ / "new note called…" | A new note, with the title as its heading |
| ״חפש…״ / "search for…" | Search opens with your words in the box |
| ״הוסף משימה…״ / "add a task…" | A checkbox line in the inbox |
| ״פתח את הפתק היומי״ / "open the daily note" | Today's note |
| ״הקרא״ / "read aloud", ״הפסק להקריא״ / "stop reading" | Reads the note aloud, or stops |
| ״לכידה מהירה״ / "quick capture" | The quick-capture window |
| ״פתח משימות״ / "show my tasks" | The tasks panel |
| ״מחק את הפתק״ / "delete this note" | Asks first, then moves the note to the trash |
| ״שמור״ / "save" | Saves |
| ״סכם״ / "summarize", ״תרגם״ / "translate" | The AI summary or translation |
| ״הכתבה״ / "start dictation" | Dictation |
| ״מצב כהה״ / "dark mode" | Switches the theme |
| ״הגדרות״ / "settings", ״לוח שנה״ / "calendar", ״תצוגת גרף״ / "graph view" | Opens them |
| ״תוכן עניינים״ / "outline", ״קישורים חוזרים״ / "backlinks" | The side panels |
| ״בדוק דקדוק״ / "check grammar" | The grammar check |

You can say "please" or "um", start with "hey Lumen", and a "ו" glued to
the first word is fine. An ordinary sentence ("save the date for the
wedding") runs nothing, because a command must be the whole sentence.

## How it's measured

The phrase list was written against 200 spoken commands, 10 per command,
in Hebrew and English. It gets all 200 of them right, and runs nothing on
20 ordinary sentences. Because the list was written for those 200, that
isn't a real test. The real one is 200 commands **recorded** by different
speakers, played through the speech model:

```sh
npm run eval:voice-commands -- --script > commands.json   # the 200 sentences to read aloud
npm run eval:voice-commands -- --dir <folder with commands.json and the recordings>
```

The target is at least 90% right. The same run is a step of
`npm run models:day -- --voice-dir <folder>`.

pages.title: Hebrew Whisper on the desktop
pages.description: Transcribe long Hebrew recordings on your computer with ivrit.ai's Whisper in whisper.cpp — one sentence per line, each time a link into the audio.
pages.md:
**Command palette → 🎙 Transcribe an audio file (with timestamps).** Pick an
audio or video file. Lumen transcribes it **on this device** and inserts the
transcript at the cursor:

```md
### team-meeting.m4a

[▶ 0:00](<attachments/2026-11-10-team-meeting.m4a#t=0,6>) Good morning, everyone.
[▶ 0:06](<attachments/2026-11-10-team-meeting.m4a#t=6,14>) Today we'll go over the budget.
```

One line per sentence. Each time is a link that plays the recording from
that point. The audio is kept in `attachments/` when the workspace is
available; without one, the times are plain text.

## Which engine transcribes

| Where | Engine | When |
|---|---|---|
| Desktop app, Hebrew | ivrit.ai Whisper large-v3-turbo (ggml) in **whisper.cpp** | once it is installed (below) |
| Browser, Hebrew | ivrit.ai Whisper turbo (ONNX, WebGPU) | a GPU with f16 and enough memory |
| Anywhere | Whisper base (WASM) | otherwise, and for other languages |

Live dictation keeps the streaming Hebrew model (Zipformer): text appears
while you speak. Whisper is used for files, where accuracy matters more than
speed of the first word. For Hebrew the language is set, never guessed.

Nothing is sent anywhere. On the desktop the audio goes to a temporary file
on your computer, `whisper-cli` reads it, and the file is removed. After the
model is on disk, transcription makes no network requests.

## Setting up the desktop engine

Lumen does not bundle the model (about 1.6 GB) or the program. You install
both once:

1. **whisper.cpp** (MIT) — on macOS: `brew install whisper-cpp`, which
   provides `whisper-cli`. Lumen finds it on your `PATH`, in the app's
   `whisper` folder, or at the path in the `LUMEN_WHISPER_CLI` environment
   variable.
2. **The model file** — ivrit.ai's Hebrew Whisper large-v3-turbo as ggml
   (Apache-2.0), into the app's `whisper` folder:
   - macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/app.lumen.editor/whisper/`
   - Windows: `%APPDATA%\app.lumen.editor\whisper\`
   - Linux: `~/.local/share/app.lumen.editor/whisper/`

Lumen only uses the exact file it was built for. It checks the size and the
SHA-256 checksum before each use, and ignores any other file. If something
is missing, the command says so and uses the browser engine instead.

:::note
The model file is not pinned in this version yet: the exact Hugging Face
repository, revision and checksum still have to be filled in
(`npm run whisper:desktop -- pin` prints how). Until then the desktop engine
is not offered and files are transcribed in the browser.
:::

## Accuracy and speed (developers)

```sh
npm run whisper:desktop -- wer --split test=<folder with fleurs.json> --model <ggml file>
```

This prints WER and CER on the Hebrew test clips (FLEURS, Common Voice),
with the same normalisation as live dictation. It also prints the speed: the
real-time factor and the minutes one hour of audio takes. The targets are WER
≤ 10% on FLEURS-he test, and under 10 minutes per hour of audio on a Mac M1.

pages.title: Citations (BibTeX)
pages.description: A ```bibtex block becomes a reference list in APA 7, Chicago author-date or MLA 9 — in English or Hebrew, with nothing sent anywhere.
pages.md:
Paste BibTeX into a ` ```bibtex ` (or ` ```bib `) block and Lumen shows a
reference list. Pick the style in the block's header; the list is sorted by
author and year, with a hanging indent. Hover a reference to see its
in-text citation.

````markdown
```bibtex
% style: chicago
% lang: he
@article{watson1953molecular,
  author = {Watson, James D. and Crick, Francis H. C.},
  title = {Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid},
  journal = {Nature}, volume = {171}, number = {4356}, pages = {737--738},
  year = {1953}, doi = {10.1038/171737a0}
}
```
````

## Styles

| Style | Reference | In text |
| --- | --- | --- |
| APA 7 (default) | Watson, J. D., & Crick, F. H. C. (1953). Molecular structure of nucleic acids: A structure for deoxyribose nucleic acid. *Nature*, *171*(4356), 737–738. https://doi.org/10.1038/171737a0 | (Watson & Crick, 1953) |
| Chicago author-date (18th ed.) | Watson, James D., and Francis H. C. Crick. 1953. “Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid.” *Nature* 171 (4356): 737–38. https://doi.org/10.1038/171737a0. | (Watson and Crick 1953) |
| MLA 9 | Watson, James D., and Francis H. C. Crick. “Molecular Structure of Nucleic Acids: A Structure for Deoxyribose Nucleic Acid.” *Nature*, vol. 171, no. 4356, 1953, pp. 737–38, https://doi.org/10.1038/171737a0. | (Watson and Crick) |

- **APA** turns the title into sentence case. Words in braces keep their
  capitals (`{DNA}`, `{Wonderland}`), as do acronyms and the first word
  after a colon. A German title (`langid = {german}`) keeps its capitals.
- **Chicago** and **MLA** keep the title as written and shorten page ranges
  by their rules (737–38). MLA drops *Company* / *Co.* from publishers and
  writes *University Press* as *UP*.

## Hebrew

`% lang: he` (or Hebrew as the interface language) changes the words, not
the order: *and* / *&* → ו (ו- before a Latin name), *et al.* → ואחרים,
MLA's *vol.* / *no.* / *pp.* → כרך / גיליון / עמ׳. Names, titles and
publishers stay as published. Each reference keeps its own direction.

## Offline

Formatting is Lumen's own rules (no citeproc, no CSL files, no download).
Whether citeproc can be used is an open licensing decision (plan 15.10);
the rules here are the fallback the plan names. Looking up a DOI is not
part of the block — it stays offline.

pages.title: Math inside Hebrew text
pages.description: Formulas in a right-to-left sentence keep their order in the editor, the preview, PDF and Word.
pages.md:
A formula in the middle of a Hebrew sentence breaks in almost every editor.
`x² + y² = r²` comes out as `r² = y² + x²`, or the `$` signs jump to the
other end. In Lumen a formula is laid out **left to right as one unit**,
wherever it sits in a right-to-left line:

```markdown
במדגם של 40 תלמידים קיבלנו $\bar{x}=12.5$ וזה נכון ב-95% מהמקרים.
```

## Where it holds

- **Preview and print (PDF).** Each formula is an isolated left-to-right
  block, so KaTeX's pieces (`a =`, `b +`, `c`) stay in order.
- **Source editor.** `$…$` is an isolated left-to-right run. The digits,
  operators and `$` signs stay where you typed them, and the cursor moves
  through the formula the way it is drawn.
- **WYSIWYG.** An inline formula is an isolated left-to-right run.
- **Line direction.** A formula does not decide a line's direction. A Hebrew
  sentence that opens with a formula, such as `$x^2$ הוא ריבוע`, is still
  right to left. `$$` display blocks are always left to right, like code.
- **Word (.docx).** Each formula becomes a Word math zone, which Word lays out
  left to right as one unit inside the Hebrew paragraph. The zone holds the
  TeX as written; Lumen does not convert it to Word's built-up equations.

## Typing formulas

- **Ctrl+M** (**⌘M** on a Mac) wraps the selection in `$…$`, or inserts `$$`
  with the cursor between. It also works with the Hebrew layout on. The
  command palette has **Insert inline formula** too.
- **No layout switch inside a formula.** With the Hebrew layout on, keys
  typed inside `$…$` in the source editor come out as the Latin letter of
  the same key: the X key types `x`, not `ס`. Outside the formula, typing is
  unchanged.

## Templates

The template gallery has three study templates, in English and Hebrew:

- **Math exam practice** (בגרות): a quadratic equation, a derivative, sequences;
- **Physics lab report**: theory, a measurement table, error analysis;
- **Statistics problem set**: descriptive statistics, a z-score, a hypothesis
  test.

## Limits

- **What counts as a formula.** A `$` followed by a space, or a closing `$`
  followed by a digit, does not open or close one. So `$5 ו-$10` is money.
  This follows Pandoc's rule, which can differ from the preview's Markdown
  parser in rare cases.
- **Typing with the Hebrew layout** works in the source editor. In WYSIWYG,
  the formula editor does not translate keys.

pages.title: Dynamic blocks reference
pages.description: The fenced code-block languages that Lumen renders as live, interactive previews.
pages.md:
Lumen's killer feature is **dynamic blocks**: write a fenced code block in markdown, and the preview renders it as a chart, diagram, table, map, or live sandbox. Every block degrades gracefully — if rendering fails, you still see the source.

## Quick-reference table

| Fence | Renders as | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| ` ```mermaid ` | Inline SVG diagram (flowcharts, sequence, gantt, class, state, ER) | Mermaid v11; lazy-loaded |
| ` ```chart ` | ECharts (line / bar / pie / scatter / heatmap / radar / boxplot / treemap / sunburst / sankey) | YAML or JSON spec |
| ` ```csv ` / ` ```tsv ` | Sortable / filterable DataTable + auto-chart suggestion | Title via `title="..."` |
| ` ```json-table ` | DataTable from a JSON array | Array of objects required |
| ` ```sql ` / ` ```pandas ` / ` ```object ` / ` ```data ` | Tabular display via the shared `DataBlock` renderer | `pandas` parses DataFrame `to_dict()` shape |
| ` ```map ` / ` ```geojson ` | Leaflet map (tile, markers, polygons, popups) | GeoJSON or YAML map-spec |
| ` ```dot ` / ` ```graphviz ` | Graphviz diagram via WASM | Rendered locally — no Kroki dependency |
| ` ```plantuml ` / ` ```puml ` | PlantUML via kroki.io | Network egress; opt out via privacy mode |
| ` ```abc ` | ABC music notation (renderable score) | Abcjs |
| ` ```model ` | 3-D model viewer (`<model-viewer>`) | GLB / GLTF |
| ` ```embed ` | Universal embed (YouTube, Vimeo, Twitter, Loom, CodePen, Spotify, Gist, …) | URL on the body line. Nothing loads until you click **Load** (or **Always allow** the site): then the player runs inside Lumen's content frame. A link to a site Lumen can't embed stays a link |
| ` ```html ` / ` ```html-preview ` | Sanitized HTML preview | DOMPurify allowlist; no JS executes in the page |
| ` ```svg ` / ` ```live-svg ` | Sanitized inline SVG preview | Same hardening as HTML |
| ` ```live-js ` | JS sandbox (Worker isolate) with console output | Stdout/stderr/error states; timeout-protected; `shared` = one REPL scope per document (see below) |
| ` ```live-lua ` / ` ```lua-live ` | Lua 5.4 (wasmoon WASM) in a Web Worker, with `print`/`io.write` output and return values | Loads on Run; self-hosted wasm (no CDN); `timeout=` ms (default 5000) |
| ` ```live-r ` / ` ```r-live ` | R (webR, WebAssembly): printed output, messages, warnings, errors and base-graphics plots | webR is GPL-3.0, so Lumen doesn't ship it: the first Run on a device offers the download (~45 MB from webr.r-wasm.org, licence shown first, every file checked against the build's checksums), then it stays on the device and works offline; `timeout=` ms (default 30000); base R + bundled recommended packages, no CRAN installs |
| ` ```live-ruby ` / ` ```ruby-live ` | Ruby 3.4 (ruby.wasm) in a sandboxed Web Worker: `puts`/`warn` output, the last value (`=> …`), errors with `block:<line>` | Loads on first Run (~30 MB, self-hosted, cached); `timeout=` ms (default 10000; a runaway loop is killed); full stdlib (`require "json"`, `set`, …), no gems; fresh VM per run; no network, storage or JS bridge |
| ` ```playground [react\|vue] ` / ` ```web-playground ` | A small multi-file web project run live: files separated by `--- name.ext ---` lines (HTML, CSS, JS, JSX, TS, JSON); Preview, a tab per file, and a Console | Runs in a sandboxed iframe on its own origin (no access to your documents); JSX / TypeScript via Sucrase; `react` / `react-dom` (18) and `vue` (3, with the template compiler) are provided offline — other packages aren't; entry is `main.*`; `height=` px |
| ` ```live-css ` | Sandboxed iframe HTML+CSS preview | `srcdoc` + sandbox flags |
| ` ```live-glsl ` / ` ```glsl ` / ` ```shader ` | GLSL fragment shader on a quad | Hot-reloads on edit |
| ` ```bibtex ` / ` ```bib ` | Citation list (formatted from BibTeX) | Click → copy citation |
| ` ```database ` | Workspace-wide database query (markdown frontmatter as the "table") | Lumen-native query DSL |
| ` ```insights ` / ` ```jsonl ` | JSONL analyzer: conclusions, freq, charts, file generators | No external model |
| ` ```code-doctor ` / ` ```fix-json ` | Malformed JSON/JSONL repair with diff + accept-fix UI | 7-pass tolerant tokenizer |

## Live JavaScript — shared scope (REPL across blocks)

By default every ` ```live-js ` block runs in its own fresh Web Worker, so nothing one block defines is visible to another. Add `shared` to the fence to turn the blocks of a document into one REPL session:

````markdown
```live-js shared
const prices = [12, 7, 30]
function total(xs) { return xs.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0) }
```

Some prose in between…

```live-js shared
console.log(total(prices))   // 49
```
````

- All `shared` blocks of the open document use **one worker**, and its global scope persists across runs and across blocks. Top-level `const` / `let` / `var`, `function` and `class` declarations become globals of that worker, so later runs and later blocks can use them. Declarations nested in blocks, functions or loop heads stay local.
- As in a browser console, running a block again may redeclare its names, and top-level `const` bindings can be reassigned by later runs.
- Blocks share state in the order they **run**. Each block runs when it renders and when you click **Run**; runs are queued and execute one at a time.
- `shared=name` (for example ` ```live-js shared=physics `) gives a separate named scope inside the same document. Different documents never share a scope.
- **Reset scope** (shown on shared blocks) discards the worker and every global in it; the next run starts fresh. Re-run the blocks you depend on afterwards.
- Sandboxing is unchanged: the worker has no DOM and no access to the page, shared mode adds no module or network-import support (the page CSP still applies inside the worker), and a run that exceeds the 8-second timeout is stopped. A timeout terminates the worker, which also resets the scope.
- An unused scope is disposed five minutes after the last shared block of that document unmounts.

## Live Lua

````markdown
```live-lua height=200 timeout=3000
local function fib(n) return n < 2 and n or fib(n - 1) + fib(n - 2) end
for i = 1, 10 do io.write(fib(i), " ") end
print()
return _VERSION
```
````

Click **Run** to execute. Nothing is downloaded until then; the ~270 KB `glue.wasm` is bundled with Lumen and served from the same origin, so it works offline and under the app's CSP. Each run gets a fresh Web Worker and a fresh Lua state:

- `print` and `io.write` stream to the output panel; values `return`ed from the chunk are shown after a `→`.
- Errors show the line (`block:2: boom`).
- A runaway loop is stopped after `timeout` ms (100–60000, default 5000) by an instruction-count hook, and the page kills the worker if it stops responding. **Stop** cancels a run.
- The Lua heap is capped at 64 MB and captured output at 200 000 characters.
- The standard libraries are available except process and file access: `os.exit`, `os.execute`, `os.getenv`, `os.remove`, `os.rename`, `io.open`, `io.popen`, `io.read`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile` and `package` are removed. Lua cannot reach JavaScript objects.

## Security & hardening

All HTML, SVG, and embed renderers funnel through `src/lib/markupSanitizer.ts`. The sanitizer:

- Strips every `on*` attribute via a prefix-matching hook (not just the named list, so future handlers like `onpointerdown` are caught).
- Blocks `style` attributes containing `expression(...)`, `url(javascript:...)`, or `behavior:`.
- Allows only image-MIME `data:` URIs (everything else, including `data:text/html`, is dropped).
- Rejects `javascript:`, `vbscript:`, and unknown protocols.

Each dynamic block is wrapped in an `ErrorBoundary` so a single broken block doesn't take down the whole preview.

## Lazy loading

Every block is `React.lazy`-imported. A block's library (Mermaid, ECharts, Leaflet, …) loads only when a note that uses it is opened, so adding block types never grows the startup bundle. That bundle has a size budget, checked on every pull request (`scripts/bundle-budget.mjs`).

## Authoring a new block

See [Plugin SDK](/plugins/sdk/) — every block is a React component registered with `registerPlugin`. The `pluginSystem` wires its fence language to a tag, mounts via `Suspense`, and routes it through the renderer pipeline.

## Web Playground

````markdown
```playground react height=260
````

pages.title: Encrypted live sharing
pages.description: Share a note live through a server that stores and relays only ciphertext, names and cursors included.
pages.md:
A note you share from Lumen goes through the collab server end-to-end
encrypted. The server keeps people to their [roles](/collab/sharing/) and
holds the room's history, but it can't read the note, its comments, or
who is in it and where their cursor is.

## What the server sees

| | Encrypted in the browser | What the server holds |
|---|---|---|
| The note | Yes (AES-GCM-256, a [ciphertext transport document](/collab/encryption/)) | Envelopes `{v, iv, ct}` |
| Comment threads | Yes, the same way (`<room>~comments`) | Envelopes |
| Presence: names, colours, cursors | Yes (since plan W2.20) | `{ "e2e": "<base64>" }` per participant |
| The room key | It never leaves the link | Nothing |
| Room name, share ids, roles, expiry | No (the server needs them) | Those, in SQLite |

The room key is in the link's fragment, after the `#`
(`#room=…&password=…&share=…`). Browsers never send the fragment to a
server, and Lumen never puts the key in a request: token requests carry
the room name, the share id or owner secret, and the operator's access key.

## Sealed rooms

An encrypted client asks for its token with `e2ee: true`, and the server
**seals** the room. From then on, for good:

- an update that writes anything except ciphertext envelopes (text, a map
  entry, a nested type, an array element that isn't an envelope) is
  refused and its connection dropped, before it reaches the room;
- a presence state with any field except `e2e` is refused the same way;
- a document that isn't ciphertext-only is never written to disk.

A room that already stores readable content (an old plaintext room) is not
sealed. To run a server that takes encrypted rooms only, set
`COLLAB_REQUIRE_E2EE=1`: every room is then sealed and plaintext clients
can't write at all.

The server checks the shape. It can't tell ciphertext from other bytes
inside `ct`; what keeps `ct` unreadable is the client, which only ever
writes AES-GCM output there.

## Encrypted presence

Each participant has two awareness instances. The editor's cursors and the
peer list use the plain one, which no provider touches. The providers sync
a transport awareness where each state is the plain state sealed under the
room key. Two values are bound into the seal:

- the participant's client id (in the GCM tag), so a relay can't show one
  participant's name or cursor as someone else's;
- a counter that only goes up, so a relay can't replay an older cursor.

A state that isn't sealed, or doesn't open with the room key, is never shown.

## Sharing needs an encrypted room

The share dialog makes links only for a room with its own key, which every
new collaboration session has. For a session joined from an old link
without a key, start a new session first.

## How it's checked

`src/__tests__/collabE2eeSharing.test.ts` runs the real server and records
every WebSocket frame both ways:

- the note's text (Hebrew and English), a comment, both participants'
  names, a cursor and the room key: **0 hits** in the traffic, the stored
  states and every file in the server's data directory. The same search on
  a room that isn't encrypted does find the text, so the check can fail;
- a plaintext writer, and plaintext presence, are refused in a sealed room;
- an edit reaches the other participant in under 150 ms (p95 over 40 edits);
- a 1 MB note with 5 participants and 1,000 random edits converges with 0
  edits lost, and a sixth participant gets the same note from the server.

## Limits

- The server still sees metadata: the room name, how many people are
  connected, when they edit and how much.
- Anyone with the link has the key. Revoking a link cuts its holder off
  from the server within seconds, but a copy of the note they already have
  stays theirs.
